Minutes of the Joint May Markets and Reliability Committees

Renaissance Framingham

May 12-14, 2026

MC Members and Alternates in attendance at the May 12-14, 2026 Meeting

Agenda Item No. 7.a – Capacity Auction Reforms Seasonal Accreditation: Resource Qualification Process Follow Up

Ms. Jennifer Engelson (ISO-NE) presented additional concepts supporting the ISO’s proposed continuous resource qualification process under CAR‑SA. The presentation addressed minimum resource size requirements, removal of the CAR‑PD Estimated Qualified Capacity (QC) process, treatment of unexpected full forced outages, and elimination of composite offers.

The ISO explained that resources with less than 100 kW of Marginal Reliability Impact Capacity (MRIC) may aggregate to form a resource meeting the 100-kW minimum threshold required to participate in a seasonal auction. Prior Forward Capacity Market (FCM) minimum‑size exceptions would not carry forward under CAR‑SA.

Ms. Engelson reviewed the rationale for the Estimated QC process under CAR‑PD, noting that it was implemented to address limited audit data and performance history for certain resources at the time of qualification. The ISO said those conditions are alleviated under the CAR‑SA framework, rendering the Estimated QC exception unnecessary.

The ISO also explained that CAR‑SA would eliminate composite offers due to the introduction of separate seasonal clearing. The presentation reviewed conforming changes to resource mapping and attribute allocation in cases where participants restructure or reconfigure resources, noting that certain resource‑level attributes would be allocated by market participants across newly formed resources, while asset‑level characteristics would transfer directly with the underlying physical assets.

In response to the presentation, the Committee:

Inquired about the numerical impact of transitioning from QC‑based thresholds to a 100 kW MRIC minimum, specifically whether the change would disqualify a material number of smaller legacy resources from standalone participation.

Expressed concern about the elimination of grandfathering provisions for legacy resources below 100 kW beginning in FCA 19, noting that deactivation could become the only viable pathway for some assets absent aggregation or reconfiguration into a distributed capacity resource structure.

Sought clarification on seasonal Maximum Capability (MCap) tracking mechanics, including confirmation that a solar resource’s baseline would continue to reset and ratchet upward over time based on rolling historical output, rather than being locked in during a low‑output seasonal window.

Raised legal and compliance concerns associated with full‑season capacity obligations when a resource has a known, extended planned outage. Members noted that clearing a six‑month seasonal obligation while physically unavailable for most of that period could create material exposure to self‑reporting or enforcement risk absent explicit Tariff treatment.

Requested that the qualification design recognize partial and planned outages, citing examples such as a 2‑by‑1 combined‑cycle facility operating in a 1‑by‑1 configuration due to long‑lead‑time equipment delays, which represent non‑speculative, verifiable capacity limitations.

Asked for clear, objective criteria to define catastrophic outage eligibility, including potential use of officer attestations, and sought clarification on how historical Equivalent Forced Outage Rate (EFORD) data would carry over or reset across restructurings or resource category changes.

In response to Committee input, the ISO:

Clarified that preliminary analysis suggests approximately 60 to 80 resources would fall below the 100 kW MRIC threshold on a standalone basis but could continue participating through aggregation under the distributed capacity resource framework.

Confirmed that while grandfathering would not continue, CAR‑SA provides pathways for sub‑100 kW assets to participate through aggregation, distributed resource structures, and monthly Bilateral or Reconfiguration Auctions to manage obligations.

Acknowledged concerns about clearing during known, extended outages, and suggested that affected resources could mitigate clearing risk by submitting higher seasonal offers and subsequently shedding obligations through monthly markets during the outage period.

Emphasized that the unexpected full forced outage process is intended as a narrow, catastrophic backstop for severe, late‑breaking physical failures occurring between the IMM cost‑workbook review and auction execution, not as a mechanism to manage routine or planned maintenance.

Committed to taking back stakeholder feedback on planned outages, partial asset limitations, and unit‑level EFORD treatment for further consideration with the IMM, noting the complexity of distinguishing verified physical limitations from potential withholding behavior.

Agenda Item No. 7.b– Capacity Auction Reforms Seasonal Accreditation: Preliminary Activity Schedule

Mr. Jeff Mislak (ISO-NE) presented a preliminary overview of the CAR￼SA activity schedule and associated market process timing. The ISO explained that implementation of a seasonal capacity construct would require modifications to existing CAR-PD, rules, and business processes to support seasonal qualification, accreditation, mitigation review, deactivation, and auction administration. The ISO noted that the schedules presented reflect current thinking and will continue to evolve as design details are refined.

The ISO reviewed proposed timelines associated with Buyer‑Side Market Power (BSMP), deactivations, the Reserve Adequacy Assessment (RAA), Installed Capacity Requirement (ICR), seller‑side market power (SSMP) mitigation, resource qualification, seasonal auctions, and monthly market processes. Mr. Mislak explained that activities currently performed on an annual basis would transition to a seasonal design, with milestone deadlines occurring closer to the applicable obligation periods. The presentation also reviewed the proposed Summer 2028 truncated transition season and explained that monthly market activities would generally retain the sequencing used under the existing FCM framework. In addition, the ISO discussed the sequencing of accreditation inputs, gas‑related assumptions and contracts, qualification determinations, and mitigation reviews required to support seasonal auction administration.

In response to the presentation, the Committee:

Asked how the baseline RAA case would be established, including the final resource mix used to calculate rMRI values and the ICR.

Questioned the timing for disclosure of key cost parameters, including Net CONE and COPT values, and whether the ISO could provide preliminary information to help participants evaluate risk and develop offers.

Raised concerns about the compressed timeline for the Summer 2028 transition season, observing that shortening the preparation window to approximately 45 days ahead of the commitment period departs significantly from historical practice and increases execution risk absent clearly codified milestones.

Sought clarification on data synchronization boundaries, specifically whether the 2027 Capacity, Energy, Loads, and Transmission (CELT) report would remain the binding load forecast input for both the Summer 2028 and Winter 2028/2029 seasonal auctions despite the age of the forecast by the start of the winter obligation period.

Expressed concern about limited visibility into the final adjusted gas constraint, and other adjustments to the demand curves, emphasizing that requiring participants to submit binding seasonal offers before final adjustments related to firm gas elections, passive demand resources, and energy efficiency are published creates material commercial uncertainty.

Questioned the operational feasibility of the three‑day catastrophic outage notification window, citing examples such as late‑stage Generator Step-up (GSU) transformer failures where coordinating IMM review and documentation within that timeframe may be impracticable.

Requested improvements to timeline graphics and process clarity, including clearer delineation of blackout periods, separation of internal clearing steps from published results timing, and clarification about treatment of non‑commercial resources under critical path monitoring.

In response to Committee input, the ISO:

Clarified that all commercial resources completing qualification data submissions by the applicable deadline would populate the baseline resource mix used for both the RAA and accreditation models.

Acknowledged the commercial challenges associated with late‑stage Net CONE and COPT visibility and said the ISO would evaluate whether preliminary guidance could be provided, while cautioning that such values may change prior to finalization.

Explained that the ICR development timeline reflects the standard data review process followed by a regulatory filing and approval window, requiring inputs to be fixed sufficiently in advance of the auction.

Confirmed that the 2027 CELT report remains the most current validated forecast available at the close of the qualification window and that fixed forecast inputs are necessary to support construction of seasonal demand curves.

Deferred detailed discussion of gas‑related demand curve adjustments and mitigation thresholds to future meetings, while committing to return in July with a clearer timeline identifying which demand curve inputs will be finalized prior to auction execution.

Explained that the catastrophic outage window is intended to provide a reporting pathway for severe physical failures occurring shortly before the auction, rather than a same‑day remediation process.

Committed to refining timeline graphics and related materials to better communicate offer windows, pivotal supplier identification, and post‑auction clearing steps, and confirmed that standard Capacity Market obligation workbooks will be conformed to the CAR‑SA structure.

Agenda Item No. 7.c – Capacity Auction Reforms Seasonal Accreditation: Non-firm Gas Capacity Demand Curve

Dr. Steven Otto presented additional design details for the proposed non‑firm gas capacity demand curve, focusing on how winter gas constraints would be reflected in capacity pricing and how firm gas contracting and monthly reconfiguration rules would interact with gas resource accreditation.

The ISO explained the gas demand curve is intended to incorporate limits on winter gas availability directly into capacity compensation so that cleared capacity more closely reflects expected fuel deliverability during winter stress conditions. The ISO summarized the proposal as consisting of five integrated elements: modeling hourly gas availability, constructing a gas‑specific demand curve, accrediting gas resources, defining firm gas contract requirements, and adjusting the demand curve to reflect firm contract designations. The presentation focused primarily on the latter two elements and their interaction with monthly reconfiguration auctions.

On firm gas treatment, the ISO said the current approach is intended to align firm gas resources with non‑energy‑limited thermal resources, reflecting a higher degree of confidence in fuel availability during winter stress. Dr. Otto acknowledged stakeholder concerns about the tradeoff between incremental reliability benefits and the cost of firm contracts, and said the ISO is evaluating potential refinements to daily pipeline requirements, LNG duration thresholds, and receipt and delivery point specifications.

For winter 2028/2029 qualification, the ISO said resources seeking to designate MRI capacity as firm would submit contracts, supporting documentation, and an officer affidavit attesting compliance with Tariff requirements. The ISO stated that it does not plan to conduct full ex ante verification of private contracts for CCP 19, instead relying on attestations and existing enforcement mechanisms, including potential clawback of CSO payments and referral processes, to deter misrepresentation while reducing administrative burden and preserving auction timelines.

For monthly reconfiguration auctions, the ISO proposed treating the non‑firm gas constraint in a manner analogous to existing export‑constrained zone mechanics. Under the proposal, limits would be tied either to the winter gas demand curve truncation point or to the quantity of non‑firm gas capacity cleared in the primary seasonal auction. The ISO noted that this gas‑related constraint would operate alongside other applicable zonal constraints, including export limits, and emphasized that the design remains preliminary and subject to refinement through further stakeholder feedback.

In response to the presentation, the Committee:

Asked how the proposed 24‑hour delivery requirement for firm gas aligns with EL3 resource treatment and how the ISO would account for physical pipeline inventory limitations when assessing deliverability.

Raised concerns about the timing and visibility of final gas demand curves, noting that valuing partial seasonal firming arrangements across individual winter months without clear ex ante guidance introduces material commercial uncertainty.

Discussed treatment of LNG incrementality, questioning whether contracted LNG should be assumed to represent entirely incremental supply or whether historical LNG volumes should be treated as baseline regional supply that shifts the demand curve.

Raised concerns regarding the treatment of LNG supply assumptions underlying the proposed β adjustment, including reliance on infrastructure such as the Northeast Gateway terminal that may not consistently contribute supply absent firm contractual commitments. Questioned whether baseline LNG availability assumptions may already reflect full utilization of existing facilities such as Everett and Canaport, and whether assuming additional incremental supply could overstate deliverability. This participant further noted that the proposed treatment could create incentives for certain firm LNG arrangements that do not materially increase available supply but nonetheless shift the gas demand curve, potentially overstating reliability benefits to consumers.

Expressed discomfort with reliance on officer attestations and post‑hoc enforcement, noting that the risk of enforcement action for inadvertent non‑compliance could deter participation absent clearer review criteria or process guidance.

Requested greater structural support from the ISO, observing that navigating complex fuel procurement requirements without pre‑registration or checklist‑based validation places a significant administrative burden on market participants.

Suggested allowing firm contract designations in monthly reconfiguration auctions, arguing that preventing resources from designating newly secured winter fuel arrangements as firm may limit flexibility during high‑stress periods.

Questioned the uniform application of firm versus non‑firm pricing across all six winter months, noting that reliability contributions during shoulder months such as November may not justify identical treatment.

Requested clarification on monthly reconfiguration auction (MRA) clearing mechanics under the gas constraint, including how overlapping zonal constraints, minimum capacity requirements, and all‑or‑nothing offers would be resolved by the clearing engine.

In response to Committee input, the ISO:

Explained that the gas availability model relies on historical delivery data to estimate regional fuel volumes available for power generation and integrates those assumptions into the RAA to reflect changing marginal reliability value.

Indicated that internal design discussions are trending toward less stringent contract requirements, while acknowledging that LNG incrementality and offer‑structure issues remain under development.

Clarified that the officer attestation requirement is intended as a standard regulatory representation of due diligence and that the ISO does not plan to review or approve private bilateral contracts on an ex-ante basis.

Outlined that questions about contract compliance would follow existing market behavior and enforcement processes if issues arise.

Maintained that firm contract designations are intended to remain anchored to the primary seasonal auction to preserve the integrity of the seasonal demand curve and ensure that compensation reflects verified winter‑block reliability value.

Clarified that MRAs would establish location‑specific clearing prices for non‑firm gas resources alongside other applicable zonal constraints, enabling localized obligation management.

Agenda Item No. 7.d– Capacity Auction Reforms Seasonal Accreditation: Gas-Only Resource Contract Requirements Follow Up

Dr. Todd Schatzki of Analysis Group presented a proposed adjustment methodology for the winter gas capacity demand curve under CAR‑SA, focused on incorporating Firm Capacity elections by gas‑only resources into the non‑firm gas constraint modeling. The presentation responded to prior stakeholder feedback and outlined a conceptual framework for how firm gas arrangements interact with non‑firm gas supply assumptions in the winter resource adequacy construct.

Analysis Group explained that gas‑only resources may elect Firm Capacity status, which removes them from the region‑wide gas supply constraint applied to non‑firm resources. Because such elections reduce the gas supply available to remaining non‑firm gas resources, the gas demand curve must be adjusted to accurately reflect marginal reliability impacts. The presentation focused on developing a consistent method to represent these changes in winter gas availability within the demand curve.

The proposal distinguished between two categories of firm gas arrangements: pipeline transportation contracts and liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal contracts. Pipeline firm transportation contracts were assumed to primarily reallocate existing gas supply away from non‑firm generators without materially increasing total regional gas availability in the short run. Under this assumption, each 1 MW of pipeline‑based Firm Capacity shifts the gas demand curve one‑for‑one to the left, reflecting a direct reduction in gas available to non‑firm resources.

By contrast, LNG‑based Firm Capacity was assumed to both displace existing gas supply and introduce some incremental gas supply to the system. As a result, LNG contracts were modeled as producing a partial leftward shift in the gas demand curve, calibrated by a factor (β) less than 1. The β parameter reflects the net effect of displaced supply minus incremental LNG deliverability, constrained by terminal send‑out limits and observed utilization during peak winter conditions.

Analysis Group illustrated the β calculation using LNG terminal send‑out assumptions, estimating that under peak winter conditions approximately 0.84 Bcf of LNG supply is delivered relative to a maximum potential send‑out of approximately 1.4 Bcf. This yields an illustrative β value of approximately 0.6, implying that each 1 MW of LNG‑based Firm Capacity shifts the gas demand curve by about 0.6 MW rather than one‑for‑one.

The presentation concluded that these adjustments are necessary to ensure the winter gas demand curve reflects only the supply available to non‑firm gas resources after accounting for Firm Capacity elections.

Dr. Schatzki emphasized that the proposal remains preliminary and subject to refinement based on stakeholder feedback, with additional discussion expected at the June Markets Committee meeting.

In response to the presentation, the Committee:

Discussed LNG incrementality, noting that terminal operators often procure LNG cargos to satisfy existing seasonal commitments rather than to supply opportunistic spot‑market sales during high‑priced winter periods.

Suggested that relying on aggregate historical profiles to infer future commercial behavior may be challenging and requested consideration of input from regional pipeline operators and LNG terminal owners about hedging practices, inventory management, and forward contracting behavior.

Inquired about treatment of prospective infrastructure changes, seeking clarification on whether baseline gas availability assumptions would adjust to reflect pipeline expansions or increased Local Distribution Company (LDC) subscriptions.

Requested clarification on the fuel‑to‑power translation methodology, including whether marginal reliability impact values are derived using fleet‑wide heat‑rate assumptions or account for resource‑specific efficiencies and dispatch characteristics.

Raised questions about the planning horizon for gas‑constraint modeling, asking whether the RAA captures supply‑side volatility over a forward multi‑year horizon or focuses gas availability assumptions on the auction year.

Noted potential interactions between cumulative LNG contract volumes and the β adjustment, observing that without a limiting mechanism, reliability impacts could persist even as aggregate contract volumes approach regional delivery constraints.

Identified baseline treatment considerations for the Northeast Gateway deepwater terminal, noting that historical tanker arrivals are infrequent and typically require advance contracting, which may warrant facility‑specific baseline treatment absent registered firm contracts.

In response to Committee input, Analysis Group:

Clarified that historical data indicates LNG terminal operators routinely sell physical molecules from storage into high‑priced spot markets during severe winter supply pressures and replenish inventories as market conditions normalize.

Agreed to consider whether baseline shift assumptions should be evaluated independently for facilities such as Northeast Gateway, acknowledging operational distinctions between structural terminal capability and contract‑driven tanker deliveries.

Explained that pipeline firm transportation contracts guarantee delivery from specific receipt points to delivery points within New England, whereas generic supply contracts without dedicated transportation rights remain subject to regional pipeline constraints.

Acknowledged the complexity of translating physical fuel quantities (Btu) into capacity‑based MW values and indicated that further detail would be developed about how demand curve shifts are implemented in the clearing engine.

Noted that a linear relationship was used for the β adjustment due to data limitations and uncertainty around more complex functional forms, and that the simplifying assumption could be refined over future auction cycles.

Observed that decomposing gas availability into discrete pipeline and LNG sub‑components may not be necessary, as the aggregate modeling framework is designed to capture deliverability limits without replicating individual commercial arrangements.

In response to Committee input, the ISO:

Indicated that additional design detail about final demand curve configuration, treatment of sunk costs in capacity offer workbooks, and settlement outcomes for non‑firm resources under binding gas constraints would be presented at the June meeting.

Noted that as CAR‑SA is implemented, observed firm contract volumes will provide a stronger empirical basis for refining baseline gas availability assumptions over time.

Confirmed that while resource adequacy modeling evaluates regional supply configurations across a forward planning horizon, gas availability and constraint profiles are calibrated specifically to the target auction year’s expected system conditions.

Agenda Item No. 7.e– Capacity Auction Reforms Seasonal Accreditation: FlatIron Energy Capital Presentation

Mr. Alex Worsley of Stack, on behalf of FlatIron Energy, presented concerns with assumptions used in ISO‑NE’s Resource Accreditation Modeling under CAR-SA, focusing on the duration and frequency of modeled MRI events, especially during winter conditions. The presentation offered that modeled MRI events frequently extend beyond observed operating experience, with nearly half of modeled winter MRI events exceeding 29 hours, despite the absence of historical capacity scarcity events lasting more than four hours. The presentation argued that these outcomes are driven by several interacting modeling inputs, including accreditation base‑case load assumptions, reliance on a limited set of extreme historical weather years, and persistence mechanics that extend stress conditions across consecutive hours.

FlatIron attributed these outcomes to several modeling assumptions, including the use of an “at‑criteria” accreditation base case that requires adding significant incremental load relative to forecasted peak demand, reliance on a small number of extreme historical weather years, and energy modeling dynamics that can extend stress conditions across consecutive hours. FlatIron emphasized that these assumptions disproportionately affect energy‑limited and storage resources by compounding accreditation impacts across Type 2 and Type 3 MRI hours, even in the absence of load shed or sustained scarcity.

The presentation questioned whether anchoring resource‑specific accreditation values to “at‑criteria” system conditions, while appropriate for determining Net ICR, is necessary or appropriate for evaluating individual resource reliability contributions. FlatIron argued that accreditation based on modeled system conditions that may not materialize could under‑accredit certain resources, increase capacity clearing prices, and distort investment signals by incentivizing a resource mix designed for extreme scenarios rather than expected operating conditions.

FlatIron suggested that accreditation based on expected near‑term system conditions in a prompt seasonal market may better reflect actual reliability contributions, improve predictability of performance risk, and preserve appropriate investment incentives, while maintaining the role of Net ICR and the demand curve in meeting regional reliability standards. The presentation concluded by identifying several open questions for further evaluation, including how to define reasonable expected system conditions, manage accreditation volatility, and address scenarios with few or no MRI events.

In response to the presentation, the Committee:

Questioned whether modeled MRI event durations appropriately reflect historical scarcity experience and operational realities.

Raised concerns that extended modeled events may understate the reliability contribution of storage and other energy‑limited resources.

Discussed whether strict use of “at‑criteria” conditions for resource accreditation is required, noting that reliability standards establish a minimum planning floor rather than a prohibition on alternative benchmarks.

Expressed concern that sharp reductions in seasonal accreditation could force capacity offer prices higher, increase procurement costs, and displace otherwise economic resources.

Highlighted potential operational implications in the DAM, noting that storage resources exiting the capacity market would no longer be subject to must‑offer obligations, potentially degrading DA price formation and complicating real‑time operations.

Suggested leveraging analytical work from the REST to refine treatment of multi‑day tail‑risk events and better align modeled stress conditions with plausible operational scenarios.

Cautioned against designing capacity accreditation exclusively around low‑probability extreme events, noting the risk that consumers could effectively pay multiple times for the same reliability product more efficiently addressed through other market mechanisms.

In response to the discussion, FlatIron:

Clarified that the proposal does not seek to alter the fundamental structure of the demand curve or its alignment with Net ICR at baseline criteria conditions but rather questions the technical justification for anchoring resource‑specific accreditation values exclusively to those same criteria points.

Agreed that incorporating REST data profiles and historical scenarios could help truncate extreme tail distributions while preserving realistic weather persistence and system behavior.

In response to the discussion, the ISO:

Reaffirmed that establishing resource accreditation at baseline at criteria conditions remains a core design principle of the capacity market design.

Agreed to review stakeholder concerns about whether alternative benchmarks could be appropriate for certain aspects of resource accreditation.

Acknowledged the suggestion to leverage REST modeling insights and said the concept would be taken back to internal technical teams for further evaluation.

Agenda Item No. 7.f – Capacity Auction Reforms Seasonal Accreditation: FirstLight Presentation

Mr. Cal Brooks of FirstLight Power presented concerns regarding ISO‑NE’s methodology for selecting and weighting winter weather years in the CAR‑SA Resource Accreditation Modeling, with a focus on how these inputs affect the frequency, duration, and severity of modeled winter reliability events.

Mr. Brooks argued that the ISO’s current weighting approach places disproportionate emphasis on both extremely cold and extremely mild historical winters, resulting in modeled conditions that overstate the likelihood and persistence of extreme winter events. As an example, he noted that the winter of 2003/04 is assigned an effective weight implying a much higher frequency than suggested by historical data, while a relatively mild winter such as 2022/23 receives the highest individual weight in the sample.

The presentation further asserted that these weighting choices materially influence accreditation outcomes by increasing the modeled duration and severity of winter stress events, which may disproportionately affect energy‑limited and storage resources. Mr. Brooks also noted an inconsistency between the winter and summer modeling samples, with winter relying on an earlier start year than summer and suggested that a more consistent methodology across seasons may be appropriate.

FirstLight proposed an alternative methodology for weather‑year selection and weighting based on detrended ERA5 temperature data and the construction of synthetic winters using multi‑day weather blocks. Under this approach, historical weather data is segmented into blocks (e.g., five‑day periods) to preserve synoptic‑scale weather patterns and inter‑day persistence, and synthetic winters are generated to better represent the probability distribution of cold‑weather events.

The proposed approach evaluates winter severity based on heating degree days and uses an optimization process to assign weights to historical years in a way that matches a target distribution derived from the synthetic dataset. Mr. Brooks explained that this approach is intended to reduce the influence of outlier years while preserving realistic tail‑event behavior and improving the statistical representation of winter risk.

Overall, FirstLight argued that refining the treatment of weather‑year selection and weighting could produce accreditation outcomes that better reflect realistic probabilities of extreme winter conditions, reduce sensitivity to a limited number of historical outliers, and improve the alignment of accreditation results with expected operating conditions.

In response to the presentation, the Committee:

Asked whether the proposed block‑based approach had been tested to estimate changes in the total number, duration, or intensity of winter MRI events relative to the ISO’s current baseline.

Noted that concerns about over‑weighting winter tail risks have been raised by multiple stakeholders and are not isolated to a single participant.

Expressed concern about the compressed timeline for moving from diagnostic analysis to actionable design decisions with consideration of alternative methodologies.

Sought clarification on the choice of five‑day blocks, asking how that interval aligns with the observed duration of regional winter weather events and whether longer block structures were considered.

Questioned whether the methodology’s focus on a limited subset of extreme blocks appropriately captures the broader distribution of winter conditions.

In response to the discussion, FirstLight:

Clarified that, absent access to ISO‑NE’s proprietary GE MARS platform, its analysis is necessarily directional, but that removing extreme outliers through a block‑based structure would naturally shorten and reduce the severity of modeled winter MRI events.

Explained that the ISO’s current weighting approach focuses on matching individual high‑load days in the extreme tail of the distribution, which may result in overfitting, whereas a block‑based optimization seeks to balance a broader distribution and preserve inter‑day persistence.

Emphasized that the objective is to establish a clear pathway toward actionable design refinement, encouraging the ISO to provide a defined schedule for stakeholder review and potential adoption of alternative tail‑risk treatments.

In response to the discussion, the ISO:

Confirmed that internal technical teams are actively reviewing alternative weather‑year weighting methodologies and related stakeholders feedback.

Indicated that updated evaluations and perspectives would be shared at the June MC.

Raised questions about the statistical validity of unconstrained synthetic winter construction, noting that random recombination of historical blocks, which are assumed to be independent, could introduce implausible weather sequences and distort aggregate severity metrics by underweighting the likelihood of more severe weather seasons.

Agenda Item No. 7.g – Capacity Auction Reforms Seasonal Accreditation: Impact Analysis – Market Clearing

Dr. Jake Fabian and Dr. Steph Kang (ISO‑NE) presented the Market Clearing Impact Analysis (MC IA) design under CAR‑SA. The ISO explained the analysis is intended to provide directional insight into differences between current rules and CAR‑SA under specified modeling assumptions, rather than to forecast prices, offers, or clearing outcomes.

The presentation reviewed the demand‑side parameters used to construct comparative clearing scenarios, including Net CONE, seasonal payment rates, MRI curves, seasonal Net ICR values, and the proposed gas‑constraint demand curve. The ISO explained under CAR‑SA, the MRI‑based demand framework is translated into separate summer and winter demand curves, each anchored to seasonal reliability criteria and calibrated to preserve expected annual cost recovery for a reference resource.

Dr. Kang explained that Net CONE serves as the central scaling anchor under current rules. Under CAR‑SA, the total annualized net cost is de‑annualized into seasonal payment rates such that expected annual revenues for the reference resource remain consistent with full cost recovery, while reflecting differences in seasonal marginal reliability value. She indicated that higher marginal reliability in winter yields higher winter payment rates relative to summer.

The presentation further described the construction of seasonal demand curves, which are scaled by seasonal payment rates. These rates are derived under the assumptions of annual cost equivalence and a constant scaling factor. The seasonal payment rates are then used to scale the seasonal MRI values so that seasonal prices equal seasonal payment rates at the corresponding seasonal Net ICRs, while maintaining a constant price cap across seasons.

The ISO introduced a regional gas‑constraint demand curve used to represent reduced marginal reliability contributions for non‑firm gas resources. Under the proposal, MRI values associated with gas deliverability constraints are translated into a separate demand curve, which may result in lower clearing prices for non-firm gas resources compared to the system clearing price in the winter.

The presentation included simplified clearing examples comparing current rules and CAR‑SA under scenarios with and without binding gas constraints. The ISO noted that, in illustrative cases where the system clears at reliability criteria, total revenues under CAR‑SA are similar to those under current rules, while seasonal price separation and gas‑related price adjustments introduce differences in revenue allocation across resource types.

The ISO emphasized that these results are illustrative and rely on simplified assumptions, including clearing at Net ICR and the absence of resource‑specific supply offers. The ISO stated that the purpose of these examples is to demonstrate demand‑curve mechanics and provide a reference point for future analyses.

In response to the presentation, the Committee:

Inquired whether Net CONE values used in the upcoming Impact Analysis will reflect tariff‑specified inflation adjustments ahead of CCP 19.

Requested clarification on the mathematical baseline of the scaling factor, including how changes in the denominator could affect the magnitude of the gas‑constraint adjustment.

Asked whether recent changes to the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) would be consistently applied across both the status quo baseline and CAR‑SA comparisons.

Sought further detail on the translation of annual Net CONE values from a QC basis into seasonal MRIC‑based payment rates.

Questioned why winter payment rates are higher in a summer‑peaking system and how administrative choices such as seasonal risk splits interact with reference‑resource MRI values and modeled event durations.

Suggested evaluating sensitivities in which seasonal risk splits are calibrated to produce uniform payment rates across seasons.

Noted minor revenue differences in baseline clearing scenarios and requested clarification on why seasonal de‑annualization does not exactly replicate current annual revenue outcomes.

Requested that future simulations expand beyond a single Rest‑of‑System (ROS) representation to include scenarios with export‑constrained zones.

Highlighted the importance of reflecting heterogeneous hedging costs and credit requirements associated with firm fuel arrangements across different market participants.

In response to Committee input, the ISO:

Confirmed that the Impact Analysis will apply tariff‑specified inflation updates to Net CONE consistently across both current‑rules and CAR‑SA models.

Explained that the regional gas constraint approach is grounded in prior delivery analysis and the same CAR-SA Capacity Demand Curve scaling factor will be applied to the entire gas constraint

Outlined the Net CONE translation process described in the accompanying Seasonal Payment Rate memo, in which total annualized net costs are reconstructed and then converted into rMRI‑equivalent seasonal payment rates.

Clarified that seasonal demand curves have already been adjusted for qualified Passive Demand Resources including energy efficiency, accounting for small baseline differences in preliminary clearing tables.

Noted that the current administrative preference is to establish Net CONE on a stable annual basis rather than recalculating values seasonally.

Emphasized that illustrative clearing prices, including the winter gas‑constraint example, are intended to demonstrate demand‑curve mechanics rather than predict actual market outcomes.

Agreed to further review baseline revenue differences and to return at the June meeting with additional resource‑class results and simulations incorporating heterogeneous capital costs.

Agenda Item No. 7.h – Capacity Auction Reforms Seasonal Accreditation: Impact Analysis: Resource Accreditation Modeling

Dr. Chris Geissler and Mr. Fei Zeng (ISO-NE) presented additional directional design information and sensitivity analysis related to the Resource Accreditation Modeling Impact Analysis under CAR‑SA. The ISO reviewed sensitivities associated with alternative seasonal Loss of Load Expectation (LOLE) splits, and their impacts on seasonal Net ICR, non‑firm gas capacity MRI curve behavior, resource mix assumptions, particularly energy‑limited and storage penetration, and updates to the treatment of energy‑limited and storage resources within the RAA modeling framework.

The ISO explained that 80/20 and 90/10 seasonal LOLE splits produced relatively limited changes to accreditation outcomes for many resource types when compared to the proposed 50/50 approach. The ISO also reviewed seasonal Net ICR and excess capacity results, noting that winter system conditions may appear less constrained in certain sensitivities prior to accounting for modeled gas deliverability constraints affecting non‑firm gas resources.

Mr. Zeng provided additional detail on modeled MRI event characteristics, including representative single-day and multi-day winter events. He explained that extended multi-day MRI events can arise when sustained high load conditions and limited opportunities to recharge energy-limited and storage resources result in repeated dispatch and energy depletion across consecutive days.

The presentation further reviewed sensitivities related to assumed gas availability, noting that higher assumed gas availability shifts the gas MRI curve to the right, reflecting higher reliability contributions and a larger quantity of non‑firm gas capacity that could be procured under those assumptions.

The ISO discussed sensitivities examining the impact of  the resource mix, particularly lower concentrations of energy‑limited and storage resources. The ISO explained modeled MRI event duration and resulting accreditation outcomes are highly sensitive to resource mix composition. Reducing assumed storage penetration resulted in higher accreditation values for remaining energy‑limited and storage resources, as charging constraints and energy limitations played a less significant role in modeled reliability events. Conversely, lower storage penetration reduced the modeled ability to shift renewable output into peak periods, lowering accreditation values for certain intermittent resources.

The ISO additionally provided an update about treatment of energy‑limited and storage resources during charging‑constrained periods. Mr. Zeng informed the Committee that the current model does not permit energy‑limited or storage resources to charge other storage resources and is evaluating potential adjustments to better reflect their contribution during charging‑constrained MRI hours. Additional detail was expected in June.

In addition, the ISO reviewed updates to RAA load modeling, including the use of a new load forecasting methodology using multiple load components and a broader set of climate‑adjusted historical weather data. Modeled weather years are selected and weighted to represent the full 70‑year distribution of load conditions, particularly in the upper tail where resource adequacy risks are most significant.

The ISO emphasized that, across sensitivities, changes to seasonal LOLE splits resulted in relatively limited differences in resource accreditation values across most resource types, indicating that modeled outcomes are primarily driven by structural system characteristics such as resource mix and assumed system conditions.

In response to the presentation, the Committee:

Expressed concern about winter load modeling parameters, noting that scaling the system to meet target LOLE criteria requires modeled winter peak demands materially above observed historical winter peaks.

Sought clarification on MRI hour classification, including whether commitment of an EL3 resource alone qualifies as a Type 2 dispatch hour.

Appreciated the inclusion of detailed hourly views and specific weather‑year profiles, noting that this granularity is necessary to evaluate how load scaling, seasonal risk splits, and historical weather weights interact within multi‑day stress simulations.

Inquired about operational constraints embedded in the multi‑day GE MARS model, specifically why the model does not show EL3 resources maximizing overnight output to fully recharge storage assets ahead of successive high‑load days.

Raised questions about the statistical fitting methodology for extreme weather tails, asking whether fitting a 70‑year sample to historical shapes may overweight outlier events and whether alternative distributional approaches could better reflect physical frequencies.

Identified potential climate‑adjustment bias between older and more recent decades, noting that climate‑adjusted load curves for recent years shift materially left and questioning whether reliance on the full 70‑year sample introduces baseline distortion.

Asked for clarification on the statistical objective function used to align historical cumulative distributions, including whether optimization focuses primarily on the extreme upper tail.

Raised conceptual questions about why a 1‑in‑70‑year extreme winter profile is incorporated into a model designed to procure capacity to a 1‑in‑10‑year LOLE standard.

Noted that the 90/10 sensitivity results suggest core reliability challenges may be driven more by structural system characteristics, such as lower winter peaks paired with higher winter capacity configurations, than by administrative seasonal risk split choices.

Requested additional detail on the steepness and non‑linear behavior of non‑firm gas MRI curves and asked whether accreditation degradation is driven primarily by absolute storage MW or by the relative share of storage within the resource mix.

Asked whether accreditation changes operate as a zero‑sum mechanism across resource classes and how removing energy‑limited resources affects baseline Adjusted Load Carrying Capability (ALCC) and remaining fleet accreditation values.

In response to Committee input, the ISO:

Clarified that a Type 2 MRI hour is strictly defined by two conditions: 1) the dispatch of storage resources to directly prevent a loss‑of‑load event and 2) depletion of stored energy during the loss of load hours; commitment of an EL3 resource alone does not meet the Type 2 criterion.

Explained that load modeling relies on actual historical weather structures rather than synthetic statistical distributions, and that the ISO seeks to match the observed historical distribution, including high-load portions of the sample.

Maintained that extending the dataset to 70 years provides a smoother, more robust representation of severe multi‑day cold snaps and avoids risks associated with shorter samples.

Confirmed that the load‑sampling process uses a mean‑squared‑error minimization objective function focused on high‑load portions of the distribution.

Clarified that the modeling does not assign probabilities to specific future events but uses historical weather paths and load weights to support meeting the 1-in-10 LOLE planning standard.

Indicated that additional detail illustrating the non‑linear behavior of gas MRI curves would be provided in subsequent materials.

Explained that accreditation sensitivity is primarily driven by the relative proportion of storage within the total resource mix due to energy‑replenishment and stored energy constraints associated with these resources.

Confirmed that when energy‑limited resources are removed from sensitivity cases, baseline ALCC declines and the resulting impacts on remaining resource accreditation are evaluated through a perturbation‑based analysis.

Clarified that accreditation adjustments as measured in MW are not zero‑sum; rather, values reflect how each resource class’s performance correlates with Expected Unserved Energy (EUE) events under changing fleet composition and outage risk.

Agenda Item No. 7.i – Capacity Auction Reforms Seasonal Accreditation: Imports Modeling and Accreditation Follow Up

Mr. Matt Brewster (ISO-NE) continued the discussion of proposed import modeling and accreditation elements under the seasonal accreditation framework, focusing on updated rules for resource-backed imports and associated qualification and accreditation requirements.

The ISO explained that resource-backed imports are associated with specific external generating units. Under current rules, the imports are accredited in a manner broadly comparable to internal resources. The CAR-SA accreditation design raises new considerations around resource performance data requirements and visibility into external system operations and constraints.

The ISO proposes further limiting external resource eligibility to non-intermittent conventional generation due to these limitations. Mr. Brewster noted this approach is intended to accommodate resource types that can be reasonably aligned with internal resource accreditation rules. The ISO indicated it would reassess eligibility at a future time following stakeholders’ interest and with inter-regional involvement.

Under the proposal, imports will submit qualification and performance attributes a few months ahead of the seasonal auction. The accredited capacity will be based on an MCap-equivalent audit measurement combined with a class-average thermal technology rMRI derived from ISO-NE’s internal modeling results.

Participants will have to affirm their resources can support the MRIC quantity for 24 hours and can elect to reduce the MRIC quantity to the level the resource can support. Once set, the MRIC will have to be offered competitively in the seasonal auction and the quantity will be fixed for the duration of the seasonal period.

The ISO reviewed additional, existing qualification requirements for imports including the demonstration of deliverability of the resource and curtailment priority for transactions. The ISO proposes officer attestation to demonstrate these requirements for CAR-SA. The ISO also proposes an eligibility requirement that ISO-NE and the source control area and any intervening control area must have a coordination agreement in effect since these are typically referenced to show transaction curtailment priority is supported.

In response to the presentation, the Committee:

Sought clarification on the scope of changes to external resource eligibility under CAR‑SA, with members emphasizing New England’s long history of importing capacity and cautioning that overly restrictive data‑visibility requirements could unintentionally exclude historic external suppliers.

Asked about the projected market materiality of the proposed exclusions, requesting an approximate magnitude to assess whether the region faces a potential supply impact on the order of tens, hundreds, or thousands of megawatts.

Raised technical questions about the use of resource‑class average MRI calculations, seeking confirmation that assigning individualized forced‑outage data to external resources aligns with the modeling mechanics described in prior accreditation appendices.

Challenged the exclusion of external energy storage resources, noting that while data‑visibility concerns may apply to intermittent resources, storage does not face the same structural barriers and may warrant differentiated treatment.

Requested clarification about wheeling and wheel‑through limitations under the proposed inter‑control area coordination agreement requirements, including whether the Tariff would prohibit capacity wheeled through more than one intervening control area.

Asked for further detail on the physical interpretation of the 24‑hour deliverability requirement, including whether participants must demonstrate a sustainable minimum output and fuel baseline across a full 24‑hour winter block.

Inquired whether non‑run‑of‑river external hydro resources with significant pondage would continue to qualify as non‑intermittent capacity under the proposed design.

Asked whether external gas‑fired resources would be required to secure firm fuel arrangements to avoid exposure to the New England non‑firm gas capacity demand curve.

Noted concern that additional firm fuel or transportation requirements could reduce the volume of external capacity available during tight winter conditions.

In response to Committee input, the ISO:

Explained that the CAR‑SA design requires detailed operational and performance data to accurately model resource interactions. This makes information‑access limitations a constraint for certain resource technologies. The conventional non‑intermittent generators have simpler modeling attributes, limited impact on accreditation results of other technologies, and their accreditation values are not particularly sensitive to their total share of the resource mix. The ISO proposes limiting eligibility to technologies where these conditions hold for the initial CAR-SA design and reassessing this later.

Clarified that the vast majority of historical external resources are categorized as non‑intermittent in their native control areas and expected to remain eligible under the proposal, such that the ISO does not anticipate a material eligibility change for external resources that historically participated.

Maintained that internal storage fleet accreditation reflects highly integrated, endogenous system dynamics that currently cannot be replicated for external storage assets operating under different dispatch and operational frameworks.

Emphasized that, unlike thermal units that can be modeled uniformly and understood to be adding equivalent reliability value, accurate modeling of storage requires greater visibility into the resource’s dispatch schedules and interactions with its native control area such as grid-charging constraints.

Agreed to review the Tariff language governing inter‑control area coordination agreements, including whether capacity imports are limited to a single intervening wheeling control area.

Clarified that the 24‑hour requirement is intended to ensure external resource capability is comparable to internal resources without energy limitations and the fuel measurement method is consistent with those for internal resources. The ISO is assessing this and will provide further detail.

Confirmed that control‑area‑backed resource rules remain largely consistent with current practices and the ISO plans to introduce a historical performance factor to determine MRIC expectations, and that non‑intermittent external hydro facilities may continue to qualify under the proposal.

Indicated that current design thinking requires external gas resources to secure contractual arrangements that render their fuel supply effectively firm from a New England reliability perspective, while acknowledging that final firm transportation boundaries are under development.

Agenda Item No. 7.j – Capacity Auction Reforms Seasonal Accreditation: Deactivations, Seasonal Offer Construction, and Mitigation

Deactivations

Dr. Zeky Murra-Anton (ISO-NE) presented proposed market power assessment and mitigation rules for resource deactivations under CAR-SA. He explained that the proposal would largely extend the existing CAR-PD deactivation mitigation rules into a seasonal construct through primarily conforming changes, while introducing targeted modifications necessary to address seasonal CCPs, season-specific economics, and multiple seasonal deactivation notification windows.

The ISO reviewed proposed changes to the conduct test and cost workbook design. Cost workbooks would continue to evaluate expected costs, revenues, and capacity prices over a minimum five-year horizon, but would now require seasonally disaggregated information. Conduct tests will be performed separately for the first two seasonal CCPs associated with a deactivation request in order to identify circumstances where a resource may seek to deactivate one season earlier than economically justified or where continued operation would require significant capital expenditures. The framework aims to capture inter-seasonal economic incentives and preserve existing market power protections.

The ISO also reviewed proposed modifications to the Portfolio Benefits Test (PBT) and associated proxy offer mitigation. The PBT would continue to evaluate whether deactivations with failed conduct tests could increase portfolio revenues but would be administered on a seasonal basis approximately twelve months prior to the applicable CCP. The revised timing may address potential “stacking” concerns associated with participants submitting multiple deactivation requests across different notification windows affecting the same CCP. Under the proposal, if a participant fails the seasonal PBT, proxy offers would apply to resources in the portfolio with failed conduct tests for the respective season. Dr. Zeky Murra-Anton also reviewed transition provisions for the initial implementation period, which would rely on FCA 18 demand and supply curves prior to availability of seasonal auction data.

In response to the presentation, the Committee:

Raised a structural question about how multi-season commercial dependencies interact with the capacity auction clearing mechanism, seeking to understand if a resource that submits an annualized cost offer in the initial season but fails to clear is forced to rationalize or deactivate the entire asset, or if the seasons are treated as commercially distinct.

Inquired whether an auction failure in a single season constitutes sufficient evidence of economic non-viability to justify a formal deactivation request under the market rules.

Requested clarification on how forward-looking resource accreditation values and changing capacity revenue streams will be integrated into the evaluation of conforming and non-conforming tariff changes.

Sought detail on the operational mechanics of partial deactivations within a seasonal construct, specifically asking how the design prevents market participants from gaming the system by submitting successive, partial deactivation requests across different seasons.

Inquired about the impact of the proposed gas constraint discounts on the Forward Capacity Market (FCM) cost allocation forecasts, asking if the ISO anticipates adjusting its capacity cost allocation methodology to reflect seasonal differences.

In response to committee input, the ISO:

Clarified that failing to clear a seasonal auction impacts the resource's immediate capacity payment rate but does not trigger an automatic or administrative deactivation of the underlying asset.

Explained that the seasonal conduct test is designed to evaluate a resource’s full financial profile across seasons, and that if a resource requires a materially unprofitable season to sustain continued operation, the Internal Market Monitor (IMM) retains discretion within the conduct test to assess cross‑season dependencies and the participant’s overall commercial narrative.

Noted that forward‑looking accreditation values are the core quantities used to evaluate future capacity revenues and inform ongoing tariff assessments.

Outlined an “auto‑pass” mechanism intended to streamline reviews: if a resource passes the IMM’s conduct test in the first season, it will receive an automatic pass for the subsequent season, reflecting the assumption that the underlying investment and cost justification is legitimate across seasons.

Emphasized that safeguards apply to the auto‑pass mechanism, noting that attempts to chain unexpected partial deactivations or materially alter resource configuration would revoke the auto‑pass and trigger a combined review of physical and economic impacts.

Seasonal Offer Construction and Mitigation

Dr. Andrew Copland and Dr. Tamara Ren (ISO-NE) presented additional design details about seasonal offer formation, seller‑side market power mitigation (SSMP), and energy market must‑offer obligations under the CAR‑SA framework. The ISO explained the proposal would largely conform the SSMP design developed under CAR‑PD into the seasonal construct, with no material changes currently planned to core mitigation tests or processes, though refinements may be considered as other CAR‑SA design elements continue to evolve.

The ISO discussed the offer review process with the IMM. Resources seeking to offer above the Capacity Offer Price Threshold (COPT) would continue to be required to submit proposed offers and supporting cost workbooks to the IMM for review. Resources may incorporate assumptions about expected CSCs and related market parameters into proposed offers, provided those assumptions are supportable through the IMM review process. The ISO also noted that it intends to continue publishing market information to support participant offer formulation and is evaluating whether additional gas related information should be made available under the seasonal design.

The presentation also discussed the proposed timing associated with COPT publication, IMM reviews, conduct tests, pivotal supplier identification, and gas‑related offer requirements. Mitigation timelines are generally intended to conform to the existing CAR‑PD design. Resources planning to incur avoidable gas contract costs as part of winter capacity offers would be required to include those costs in IMM‑reviewed cost workbooks if seeking to offer above the COPT.

The ISO further explained proposed conforming changes to energy market must‑offer requirements under CAR‑SA. Energy market offer obligations would generally be based on the proportion of a resource’s MRIC receiving a CSO and applied to the resource’s MCap or equivalent capacity value, while continuing to account for physical available.

The presentation reviewed application of these principles to storage, Active Demand Capacity Resources (ADCRs), Distributed Energy Capacity Resources (DECRs), and hybrid resources. The proposal preserves existing physical availability principles while adapting must‑offer obligations to the seasonal accreditation construct. The ISO proposed adding Tariff provisions authorizing the IMM to review allocation of MRIC across hybrid resource components to ensure such allocations are supported by underlying physical or economic justification.

In response to the presentation, the Committee:

Inquired about application of the pivotal supplier test under a binding gas constraint, asking whether a fleet of gas resources whose marginal reliability contribution is fully discounted could yield a zero‑capacity clearing price.

Requested that the ISO develop a step‑by‑step illustrative example demonstrating how a natural gas resource would construct a winter seasonal capacity market offer based on avoided‑cost principles, including treatment of gas contract costs.

Sought clarification about compliance obligations for gas resources that fail to clear against the seasonal demand curve, asking whether a resource receiving a zero CSO would remain subject to any Day‑Ahead energy market must‑offer requirements.

Raised questions about IMM review criteria for hybrid resources, requesting illustrative guidance on what constitutes an appropriate internal allocation of MRIC across constituent assets.

Challenged the necessity of explicit new Tariff provisions for hybrid resource reviews, questioning whether the IMM already possesses sufficient authority under existing mitigation rules to address potential gaming or physical withholding.

Requested clarification on how energy market must‑offer obligations and outage‑scheduling requirements apply during critical winter months to resources that do not hold a CSO.

In response to Committee input, the IMM:

Clarified that resources without a CSO are not subject to mandatory Day‑Ahead energy market must‑offer requirements or standard daily mitigation penalties.

Emphasized that if an economic resource without a CSO fails to offer its available capacity into the energy market, the IMM would initiate a physical withholding review to assess whether the behavior constitutes anti‑competitive conduct.

Suggested that participants refer to the energy market must‑offer design adopted in late 2022 for additional context about winter‑period operational reviews.

In response to Committee input, the ISO:

Agreed to develop and present a comprehensive compliance example illustrating how a gas resource would construct a seasonal capacity market offer using avoided‑cost principles.

Confirmed that under current design assumptions, Day‑Ahead energy market must‑offer obligations are strictly conditional on a resource holding a valid CSO; a resource that does not clear the capacity auction would not carry a baseline Day‑Ahead energy offer requirement.

Explained that proposed hybrid‑resource Tariff provisions are intended to establish a transparent and reviewable framework for IMM oversight, rather than to signal any deficiency in existing monitoring authority.

Verified that broader energy market must‑offer parameters and outage‑scheduling requirements would continue to apply uniformly during the winter season, regardless of a resource’s capacity obligation status.

Agenda Item No. 7.k – Capacity Auction Reforms Seasonal Accreditation: Capacity Market Cost Allocation

Dr. Ernesto Guzman (ISO-NE) presented the final component of the CAR-SA capacity market cost allocation design, focusing on how the non-firm gas capacity pricing adjustment is incorporated into seasonal cost recovery in the winter.

The ISO reiterated under CAR-SA, capacity costs are allocated to Capacity Zones based on seasonal coincident contribution to system peak demand and seasonal Capacity Clearing Prices. The update addresses how the non-firm gas capacity price separation, arising from the winter gas constraint,  is translated into a system-wide cost adjustment.

Because non-firm gas resources clear at a discount due to the modeled gas constraint, the resulting price separation generates a credit that is treated as a reduction to total winter capacity auction costs prior to allocation. This ensures that the cost impact of the gas constraint is reflected at the system level before zonal allocation occurs.

The adjusted net auction cost is then allocated using the standard seasonal capacity allocation framework based on zonal capacity obligations and clearing prices. Zonal costs are converted into charge rates and applied to load through capacity load obligations, consistent with the broader CAR-SA cost allocation structure.

The ISO noted that this credit also flows through related capacity market charges, including self-supply adjustments and transmission-related capacity cost components, ensuring consistency across the full set of CAR-SA capacity cost mechanisms.

In response to the presentation, the Committee:

Inquired about the administrative treatment of the FCM cost allocation forecast, asking if the proposed seasonal mechanics and regional gas constraint discounts would be integrated as a conforming change into the standard forecasting workbooks that market participants rely on for corporate budgeting.

Emphasized the importance of understanding how seasonal cost allocation changes would flow through existing ISO budgeting and forecasting tools.

In response to Committee input, the ISO:

Acknowledged the importance of the cost allocation forecast for participant budgeting cycles.

Committed to reviewing the technical adjustments internally and returning to the committee with a definitive update on how these forecasting workbooks will be updated going forward.

Agenda Item 5.a – DECR Modeling & Accreditation

Dr. Ben Chenault (ISO-NE) discussed Distributed Energy Capacity Resources (DECR) modeling and accreditation.

In response to questions, the following comments were provided:

No DECRs cleared in FCA 18.

Existing Active Demand Capacity Resources (ADCRs) can, but will not be required to, requalify as DECRs, because Demand Response Resources (DRRs) may participate in the capacity market as ADCRs or DECRs.

The ISO provided analysis around highest load days at a prior MC/RC meeting. Based on this analysis, the ISO has not received any feedback to suggest adjusting the data set from the 15 highest load days over last three like seasons.

A vote we be taken at a future meeting.

Agenda Item 5.b – Seasonal Tie Benefits Follow-Ups

Ms. Manasa Kotha (ISO-NE) continued discussion on seasonal tie benefits.

In response to questions, the following comments were provided:

Capacity Import Capability (CIC) is unlikely to change frequently. The only recent changes have been associated with the New Brunswick tie.

The annual sensitivity study threshold will be used during intervening years if there is a change in CIC.i  . The ISO is not proposing a percentage-based threshold for changes in CIC.

In past years, the ISO has performed sensitivity analyses on large supply changes in neighboring control area models and found that they do not have a substantial impact on the outcome of the study.

If necessary, the ISO can update seasonal tie benefits values on an off-cycle basis via a 205 filing.

Summer and winter tie benefits are calculated simultaneously in a single seasonal tie benefit study.

The ISO in its seasonal tie benefits study  aligns its model to NYISO’s model triennially utilising the Long-Range Adequacy Overview (LRAO).

A vote we be taken at a future meeting.

Agenda Item 5.c – Capacity Zone Formation

Ms. Manasa Kotha (ISO-NE) discussed capacity zone formation in a seasonal construct.

In response to questions, the following comments were provided:

Current objective criteria testing uses existing capacity resources to evaluate if a zone is triggered as import constrained. For export constrained, criteria testing not only includes existing capacity resources but also includes Show of Interest (SOI) capacity to see if there will be more capacity that can clear.

There are no major proposed changes to the Transmission Security Analysis (TSA) for CAR-SA.

The Installed Capacity Requirement (ICR) and accreditation models do not use the zonal interfaces.

Removing gas-only resources casts a wide net of resources to send the signal that price separation can occur during an auction. This adjustment focuses on the supply side of the equation but demand and transmission capacity also need to be considered. Demand is historically lower in the winter and will offset some of the adjustments to the supply side. Transmission elements have higher ratings in the winter (e.g., Case Study 1 20F ratings once Order No. 881 goes into effect), which can result in higher interface transfer limits.

Short-term firm arrangements for gas supply would not be known in time for objective criteria testing. The ISO needs to take back the question around longer-term firm fuel arrangements.

The ISO will consider how external Elective Transmission Upgrades with Capacity Network Interconnection Service will be modeled when evaluating zones.

Participants made the following comments:

A member of the Alternative Resource sector noted discomfort with the removal of all gas-only resources, stating that they would be more comfortable with a subset of gas-only resources being left in the model.

Participants from the Supplier and End User sectors requested that the ISO apply the proposed methodology to FCA 18 to provide an example of the impact of the removal of gas-only resources.

A member of the Supplier sector stated they believe all zones should be modeled at all times to allow for the opportunity for price separation.

A vote we be taken at a future meeting.

Agenda Item 11.0 – Other Business

The next Reliability Committee meeting will be on June 25, 2026.

The meeting adjourned at 2:32 PM.

Agenda Item No. 2.0 – Capacity Auction Reforms – Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA)

Mr. Kevin Coopey (ISO-NE) discussed deactivations in a seasonal framework to align with the deactivation processes approved by FERC on March 30, 2026. The ISO proposes that there will be two Deactivation Notification Deadlines in each year, rather than one in a prompt, annual framework. The notification deadlines will align with the proposed CAR-SA seasons.

In response to questions, the ISO made the following statements:

Under a seasonal framework, resources could have up to a 180 day (~ 6 months) waiting period to submit a deactivation notification.

Additional changes to deactivation market power mitigation will be discussed at the May Markets Committee meeting.

In reference to questions regarding accelerated deactivation requests, the ISO noted that it requires up to 90 days to complete full market power and reliability review.

The ISO envisions providing public information on the ISO website when the reliability review is complete.

If the ISO identifies a reliability need during its review, Attachment K processes would be triggered. In this circumstance, a resource may be retained until the reliability need has been resolved.

If the ISO determines a resource is needed for reliability, it could still reject the ISO’s request and proceed with retirement.

The ISO confirmed all resources would follow the same notification process and stated that more details would be shared during the participant readiness process. The ISO noted that the initial notification deadline may look different from subsequent deadlines, as new software is being developed.

The following comments were issued:

Stakeholders noted support for the ISO’s proposal to increase the number of Deactivation Notification Deadlines to align with a seasonal framework.

A future vote will be taken on this item.

At its June 9-10 meeting, the NEPOOL Markets Committee (the “Markets Committee”) 
will be asked to direct the NEPOOL Generation Information System (“GIS”) Operating Rules 
Working Group (the “Working Group”) to consider potential changes to the GIS to reflect 
improvements to the Certificate Statistics Public Report (the “Report”). This change is requested 
by the Freedom Companies, C.N. Brown Electricity, LLC, Plainfield Renewable Energy, LLC 
and Maine Power LLC. 
 
This request would expand generator location disclosures on the Report. Currently, the 
columns for New York (NY ISO control area), Maritime Provinces (including portions of Maine 
not in the Control Area), and Quebec (the “Columns”) are only displayed under the Statistic By 
Eligibility & Location view. This request would enhance the Report to include the Columns under 
the following report statistic views: By Eligibility, By Fuel, By Fuel Attributes, By Other 
Attributes, and By Renewable Fuel Type.  
 
The Markets Committee is not being asked to vote on any changes to the GIS at this time.  
Rather, the Markets Committee is only being asked to refer the item outlined above to the 
Working Group so that the Working Group can further discuss and determine if GIS Operating 
Rule revisions are needed and if the Working Group supports the proposal.  Of course, if the 
Markets Committee decides to refer these issues to the Working Group, its input at this time 
would be appreciated, as it may help direct the Working Group’s discussions.

RE: 
GIS Referral Maine and Rhode Island RPS Operating Rule Changes   
 
At its June 9-10, 2026 meeting, the NEPOOL Markets Committee (the “Markets 
Committee”) will be asked to direct the NEPOOL Generation Information System (“GIS”) 
Operating Rules Working Group (the “Working Group”) to consider changes to the GIS and the 
GIS Operating Rules (the “Rules”) to provide that air emission data is not required to be entered 
in the GIS in order for biomass and landfill gas facilities to be denoted as eligible for the Maine 
and Rhode Island Renewable Portfolio Standards (“RPS”). This change was requested by the 
Freedom Companies, C.N. Brown Electricity, LLC, Plainfield Renewable Energy, LLC and 
Maine Power LLC. 
 
 
Currently, the Maine and Rhode Island RPS laws do not include air emission standards 
for biomass and landfill gas generators.1 Rule 2.5(e) requires that emissions data for generators 
(other than Zero Emissions Generators) be entered into the GIS by the fifth calendar day 
preceding each quarterly Creation Date, and the GIS does not denote Certificates as RPS-eligible 
if the required emissions information is not provided. The requested Rule change would remove 
the requirement to enter emissions data for “Class I” treatment for landfill gas and biomass 
generators in Maine and Rhode Island only.   
 
Class I treatment would still be denied for failure to enter actual air emissions in Connecticut, 
Massachusetts, New Hampshire and Vermont. 
 
The Markets Committee is not being asked to vote on any changes to the Rules at this 
time.  Rather, the Markets Committee is only being asked to refer the item outlined above to the 
Working Group so that the Working Group can further discuss and determine the Rule revisions 
needed if the Working Group supports the proposal.  Of course, if the Markets Committee 
decides to refer these issues to the Working Group, its input at this time would be appreciated, as 
it may help direct the Working Group’s discussions. 
cc:  NEPOOL GIS Operating Rules Working Group  
 
1 See 65-407 Me. Code R. CH. 311, § 2 (Renewable Portfolio Requirements for applying for Maine’s RPS 
program do not include emissions data for biomass or landfill methane gas facilities); and 810 R.I.C.R. 40-05-2.5 
(providing that biomass facilities using Eligible Biomass Fuels and maintaining compliance with current air permits 
are Eligible Renewable Energy Resources and landfill gas is considered “Eligible Biomass Fuel”)

The ISO is requesting a vote on proposed Tariff revisions that make targeted changes to adjust the 
Day-Ahead Ancillary Services (DA A/S) Market in response to recommendations from the ISO’s 
Internal Market Monitor (IMM). 
By way of background, in February 2026 the IMM recommended incremental design adjustments to 
improve the cost effectiveness of the DA A/S market, based upon its observations and analysis of the 
first year of the market’s operation.1 The ISO reviewed and agreed with the recommendations, and 
proposed  targeted updates to the non-performance factor (NPF), adding a floor to the strike price 
based upon indicative characteristics of a distillate-fired combustion turbine (CT), and adjusting the 
Forecast Energy Requirement (FER) Demand Quantity. 
The reduction to the NPF from 120% to 115% was reviewed and discussed by the Reliability 
Committee on April 22, 2026 and put into effect on April 30, 2026 for the May 1, 2026 Operating Day.  
Given the improvements in resource performance and additional market and operational changes 
that incentivize and support resource responsiveness, a reduction to the NPF better aligns reserve 
requirements with demonstrated system needs without compromising reliability.  
The proposed strike price floor better aligns the strike price with the short run marginal costs of the 
class of resources observed to have cleared a significant share of DA A/S awards. This proposal 
balances tradeoffs by reducing the range between short run marginal costs and the strike price (in 
which such resources would not physically cover their position), reducing closeout cost risk while 
preserving incentives when system conditions are tightest.  The ISO also proposes to implement a 
floor of $3/MWh on the Impact Test Threshold, to address the potential for over-mitigation in hours 
when expected closeout is very low, and market power is not a significant concern. 
The ISO proposes reducing FER Demand Quantity by the forecasted but uncleared real-time front-
of-the-meter wind and solar generation to avoid over-procurement and better align the Day-Ahead 
Market with the Reserve Adequacy Analysis process, the ISO’s longstanding reliability evaluation.
