Introduction  
The Massachusetts Attorney General’s Office (“Massachusetts AGO”) appreciates ISO New 
England’s (“ISO-NE” or the “ISO”) recent responsiveness to urgent stakeholder concerns about 
the alarming and unsustainable cost of the DA A/S market through its first year.1  The 
Massachusetts AGO likewise appreciates the Internal Market Monitor’s (“IMM”) review and 
analysis of the DA A/S market’s performance in its first year, and is grateful to both the ISO and 
the IMM for offering thoughtful, actionable, incremental solutions to mitigate some of the cost 
impacts of this market going forward.  The Massachusetts AGO strongly supports the ISO’s 
expeditious efforts to implement the IMM’s February 2026 recommendations for targeted changes 
to the DA A/S market,2 and encourages both the Markets and Participants Committees to support 
the ISO’s efforts to implement these recommendations.

$1.2 billion.3  Taking into consideration the effect of DA A/S on Day-Ahead (“DA”) energy costs,

Recommended Targeted Adjustments 
First, the ISO proposes to reduce the Non-Performance Factor (“NPF”)14 for Total Ten-Minute 
Reserves (“TTMR”) from 120 percent to 115 percent.15  It was last set prior to several significant 
market design changes implemented by the ISO, including the capacity market Pay-for-

consumers have been paying higher prices for larger quantities of reserves than the amount 
indicated as necessary to meet reserve requirements.  Adjusting the NPF down to 115 percent will 
incrementally reduce the required quantity of reserves procured in the auction and put downward 
pressure on prices.  This change does not require a vote or Tariff change and the NPF adjustment 
has already been implemented by the ISO.17

Second, the ISO proposes to adjust the FER18 downward to reflect the full expected real-time 
contribution of Front-of-the-Meter (“FtM”) renewable resources.19 As originally designed, the 
FER treats Behind-the-Meter (“BtM”) resources fundamentally differently from FtM renewables. 
Specifically, FER nets out expected BtM generation but does not consider expected FtM 
generation (which is based on the same forecast models as BtM generation).  Only the FtM 
generation that clears the DA market is counted toward FER, even though the ISO anticipates and 
relies on the full expected FtM generation with the same confidence as BtM generation.20  As a 
result, the DA A/S market clears higher quantities of energy and reserves (at higher prices) than 
indicated by the ISO’s expectation of supply and demand conditions.21 Reducing FER by FtM 
renewable generation forecasted in real-time but not cleared in the DA market will reduce 
consumer costs by decreasing the quantity of DA energy and EIR procured in the auction, and put 
downward pressure on prices.  
Third, the ISO proposes to set a Strike Price floor based on the indicative characteristics of an 
efficient Combustion Turbine (“CT”) generator.22  This proposal is based on the ISO’s finding that 
over the first 11 months of DA A/S operations, CT units made up the majority of cleared DA A/S 
resources, and the average short-run marginal costs (“SRMC”) of those units were more than three 
times the average Strike Price over that period.  When marginal costs so drastically exceed the 
strike price, performance incentives are muted, closeout risk increases (leading to higher offer 
prices and market clearing prices), and market participation is discouraged.23  The ISO’s current 
proposal would set a Strike Price floor based on an efficient CT unit and the lowest-price distillate 
fuel used by resources that have cleared the market.24  The ISO estimates that its Strike Price floor 
proposal will have the most impact during low-load hours, and less of an impact at increasing load 
hours, which reduces overall costs while better aligning SRMC with the Strike Price, and preserves

Conclusion 
As a result of the ISO’s proposed changes, consumers will receive the same products from the DA 
A/S market at a lower cost, and resources will still receive strong (but more efficient) incentives 
to perform.  Together, these proposals have the potential to provide meaningful relief to 
consumers.  Indeed, these adjustments would have saved consumers an estimated $292 million—
30 percent of incremental DA A/S costs—if they had been in place from the outset of the DA A/S 
market.26  Given the current energy affordability crisis, the Massachusetts AGO urges the Markets 
and Participants Committees to take the opportunity to provide customers with this needed cost 
relief.  
The Massachusetts AGO appreciates the ISO prioritizing the implementation of these targeted 
changes as soon as practical.  In addition to these targeted solutions, the Massachusetts AGO looks 
forward to the IMM’s one-year lookback at the DA A/S market.27  The Massachusetts AGO 
expects that this “competitiveness” report will provide a comprehensive cost-benefit analysis of 
the DA A/S market and help identify any other potential reform areas to ensure that the DA A/S 
market delivers the benefits of ancillary services cost-effectively. The Massachusetts AGO looks 
forward to continued stakeholder engagement on DA A/S at the June Markets and Participants 
Committee meetings and beyond.

Background on Transitions
• For major capacity market changes, the ISO has often 
included a transition mechanism to provide a glide path from 
the current to the proposed rules over several auctions
• Reduces the extent to which market outcomes change 
dramatically in a single auction, thereby providing a degree of 
stability to the region and allowing participants to adjust to 
the rule changes over a series of auctions
• Continues to provide sound investment signals by proposing 
the fully phased in design

4
Transition Objectives
• Glide Path: Simply put, the transition should move the market from 
where it is today to where it proposes to go over a series of auctions
– Allows participants (and the ISO) to learn about the new design before its full 
effects are felt
– This may be done incrementally across several auctions, where the 
transition moves towards the final proposal
• Simple and Implementable: The transition mechanism should be 
simple to design, understand and implement
– Does not require continued use of legacy processes and systems that will be 
discontinued under the proposed design
– Can be in tension with providing a glide path

• Unlike some previous capacity market changes, the CAR reforms 
include a number of substantive changes, including to:
– Auction timing
– Auction seasonality
– Capacity accreditation
– Winter gas constraint
• There are complex interactions between these items!
• Will therefore need to carefully consider what design elements are 
included in the transition (and how)

Accreditation – Transition resource accreditation values from their current QC-based

Capacity Commitment Periods
II.
System and Zonal Demand Curves – These parameters will need to be updated to ensure

accreditation changes and transition objectives
III.

constraint

• Instead, the transition would use a proxy QC value that 
estimates resource-level QCs from resource parameters that 
will already be calculated and known to the resource and ISO
• Next: Current thinking regarding how proxy QC would be 
calculated

[Page 14]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
14
Accreditation Transition: Mechanics (cont.)
• For each resource type, calculate the average ratio of QC 
to MCap for summer and winter
– Current thinking is to do these calculations before the transition period 
begins and fix these ratios throughout the transition period
• For each transition season and resource, multiply the 
applicable ratio by the resource’s relevant seasonal MCap 
value to get resource-specific proxy-QC values

[Page 15]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
CURRENT THINKING: DEMAND CURVE TRANSITION
15

[Page 16]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
16
Demand Curve Transition
• ISO is assessing how the transition mechanism would apply to the demand 
curves
• Observation: It would not make sense to use the MRIC-based demand curves 
proposed for the final design in this transition, as this would result in the 
demand curve being shifted significantly further to the left than the supply curve 
during the transition period, resulting in:
– Low clearing prices due to this misalignment
– Potentially poor system reliability as it would presume the auction is buying MRIC, when in 
fact, it is buying a less reliable capacity product that is a hybrid of MRIC and QC
– Recall: In the earlier example, the resource could sell 90 MW of transition capacity but only 
had 70 MW of MRIC; if we buy 70 MW from this resource in the transition, it represents 78% 
of its transition capacity, rather than 100%
• The ISO plans to return with more information regarding its proposed demand 
curve transition at future meetings

[Page 17]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
CURRENT THINKING: GAS CONSTRAINT TRANSITION
17

[Page 18]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
18
Gas Constraint Transition
• The ISO is assessing whether to include a transition to the gas constraint that 
may allow for the procurement of more non-firm gas during the transition period 
than under the final CAR-SA proposal
• This design element is inherently complex for multiple reasons:
– Unlike accreditation and capacity demand, there is not a clear starting point to transition 
from, as the region does not currently employ a gas constraint 
– The gas constraint interacts with other parameters and auction outcomes (e.g., capacity 
demand, clearing outcomes) in nuanced ways
– As part of the CAR-SA design, the ISO is proposing modifications to the interaction between 
firm contracts and the constraint, which may lessen the need for such a transition on this 
element 
• The ISO will provide more information regarding its thinking on this element, and 
design details if it chooses to include a transition to the gas constraint at a 
future meeting

ISO-NE PUBLIC
19
Conclusion and Next Steps
• The ISO intends to propose a transition mechanism as part of its 
CAR-SA proposal
• Today, the ISO has offered its current thinking regarding the 
objectives, scope, and timing of such a transition
• It has also outlined its current thinking about how the transition may 
phase in the resource accreditation values
• Plan to provide more information regarding the ISO’s thinking on 
transition demand parameters at future stakeholder meetings
• Stakeholder feedback is welcome
– Please email comments and questions to the Markets Committee 
Secretary, Jasleen Singh, Jsingh@iso-ne.com by June 24, 2026

Purpose of the IA & Results Interpretation
•
The Resource Accreditation Modeling IA aims to use the RAA 
model outcomes generated based on a set of input 
assumptions to provide the region with directional information 
about the CAR design 
•
These IA results should not be interpreted as ISO predictions or

•
Modeling multiple cases will help stakeholders develop their

range of potential conditions

•

•

–
The potential for updates to the design based on continued ISO assessment and discussion with

–

Recap of CAR-SA RAA Load Modeling
•
The ISO seeks to capture a broad range of weather variability and its 
impacts on hourly load in the RAA model and builds this load model 
using 70 years of climate-adjusted historical weather data
– These hourly load data form the foundation for key load forecast parameters, 
such as 50/50 and 90/10 annual and seasonal peaks
•
Due to limitations on developing IPR wind and solar profiles, a subset 
of historical weather years is used in the RAA model
– 2007–2023 for summer
– 2000/01–2022/23 for winter
•
These weather years are assigned optimized weights to emulate load 
variability across the full 70-year period
– The weighting approach ensures the modeled weather years are as 
representative as possible of long-term weather-driven load variability

[Page 7]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
7
Modeled Load Years Represent 70-Year Weather-Driven 
Load Variation
•
Modeled weather years are representative of the broader 70-year 
weather distribution for both summer and winter
– These years span a range of conditions across the upper tail of the 
distribution, where resource adequacy assessment is most relevant
– Optimized weights improve the alignment with the 70-year distribution

Hourly Loads
•
Solar output has a weak correlation with hourly load during 
winter, unlike summer, reducing the need to pair load with solar 
profiles
– Winter peak loads historically occur in early evening hours, when solar 
output is minimal or zero
•
This enables testing an alternative approach using a full 70-year 
set of winter hourly load profiles as a sensitivity test of the ISO’s 
proposed load modeling framework
•
The ISO conducted a sensitivity analysis with the IA near-term 
base case to assess impacts on demand parameters, key 
reliability metrics, and overall resource accreditation outcomes

Sensitivity Analysis
Key Takeaways
• The selected load years with optimized weights closely 
emulate the outcomes of explicitly modeling the full
70-year set of hourly load data
• Across approaches, results are highly consistent, 
including net ICR, core reliability metrics (e.g., LOLE,

• These results provide strong support that the proposed

[Page 14]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
14
ISO Will Continue to Use the Proposed Load 
Modeling Framework for CAR-SA
•
The ISO does not propose modeling all 70 years of winter hourly loads for CAR-SA
•
The current load modeling framework adequately represents long-term (70-year) 
weather-driven load variability and its impacts on demand parameters, reliability 
metrics, and resource accreditation
•
The ISO’s proposed approach significantly reduces implementation complexity and 
effort, while maintaining analytical robustness
–
Explicitly modeling 70 years would require additional setup and post-processing
–
And require substantially more load profiles across all zones, increasing model size and 
complexity for zonal requirements and demand curve development
–
The proposed approach avoids the need to develop additional correlated profiles (e.g., for PDRs)
–
And preserves modeling flexibility and scalability, allowing future alignment of load with solar 
resource profiles when correlation becomes important
•
For example, if winter peak demand shifts from evening to morning hours 
•
The ISO will continue to evaluate the robustness of its modeling framework as the 
load forecast evolves

[Page 15]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
ISO’S ASSESSMENT OF ALTERNATE LOAD 
MODELING APPROACHES
15

[Page 16]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
16
FirstLight’s Proposal
• FirstLight proposed an alternate approach for weighting 
weather years as outlined in its May MC presentation 
• The ISO has performed a high-level assessment on 
FirstLight’s proposed approach and the potential resulting 
impacts on net ICR and accreditation outcomes of energy 
limited and storage resources

[Page 17]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
17
ISO’s High-Level Assessment
•
The FirstLight proposal offered alternate methodologies and 
durations by which to measure weather severity/patterns, 
including discrete sub-seasonal blocks
•
However, when the weather associated with each block is 
treated as independent, it ignores important correlations 
between these blocks and temporal heterogeneity, which are 
inherently captured in the 70 years of historical data
– The last day of block b1 and the first day of block b2 are treated as 
independent, even though they are likely to be highly correlated
– Longer-term weather correlations that may extend beyond the 
duration of a single block

[Page 18]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
18
ISO’s High-Level Assessment (cont.)
•
Ignoring these broader correlations and temporal heterogeneity 
will tend to understate the likelihood of severe winters because:
– They assume that the likelihood of severe weather in block b2 does not 
depend on the weather in b1
– However, in practice, if there is severe weather in b1, it is then more 
likely that there is also severe weather in b2
•
This means the likelihood of severe weather occurring in both b1 
and b2 (a severe winter) is greater than a methodology 
assuming these blocks are independent would predict
•
A simple numerical example illustrating this point is provided in 
the Appendix

ISO-NE PUBLIC

23
Key Takeaway
•
ISO aims to capture the impact of high load conditions, which is most 
relevant to the resource adequacy assessment, by using the RAA load 
model to represent the probability of these conditions, based on 
hourly load data derived from 70 years of climate-adjusted historical 
weather. These data also form the basis for key load forecast 
parameters
– In practice, a subset of load years with optimized weights is used to replicate 
the outcomes of explicitly modeling all 70 years
•
ISO remains open to evaluating alternative methodologies and 
continuing to engage with stakeholders; however, it is not currently 
adopting approaches that assign different weights across all 70 years, 
for example:
– Selectively excluding specific years as outliers

[Page 24]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
“AS IS” VS “AT CRITERION” CONDITION FOR 
ACCREDITATION
24

[Page 25]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
25
Objectives of Capacity Market
•
As the ISO has explained consistently during CAR, the 
objectives of the capacity market are to ensure we have 
sufficient capacity to meet the region’s 1-in-10 resource 
adequacy standard on average over time, and that this capacity 
is procured in a cost-effective manner
•
We refer to the conditions that satisfy these objectives as the 
“at criteria” conditions
•
Given that the capacity market’s primary objective is to help the 
region meet the 1-in-10 standard, it is sensible that the study 
assumptions are consistent with that objective
•
It helps guide the region towards meeting this objective

[Page 26]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
26
“At Criteria” Condition: A Core Design Element 
for Capacity Market
•
Under the Forward Capacity Market (FCM), the use of “at criteria” assumptions has been 
discussed at length with stakeholders and FERC
•
Key system parameters are developed under the “at criteria” condition, where supply and 
demand are balanced to meet the LOLE reliability target (which aligns with the “at criteria” 
condition), including:
–
Net CONE
–
Net ICR
–
Capacity zone requirements
–
Tie benefits
•
While the current QC metric does not specifically take a position, the ISO proposes to use this 
same set of “at criteria” assumptions for calculating resource accreditation values under CAR-SA
•
The ISO’s proposed approach ensures:
–
Consistent alignment with the reliability standard
–
Consistent signals of evolving system capacity needs
–
Proper reflection of seasonal differences in reliability risk

[Page 27]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
27
“At Criteria” Condition: A Core Design Element 
for Capacity Market (cont.)
•
Some stakeholders have indicated an interest in potentially 
developing resource accreditation values based on an “as is” 
system
•
ISO proposes that the “at criteria” assumptions informing 
resource accreditation are consistent with those used 
elsewhere in the capacity market parameters development for 
the reasons noted above
– An “at criteria” design is generally adopted by other ISOs
•
Using “at criteria” assumptions consistently will help ensure the 
capacity market satisfies its resource adequacy objective, and 
provides consistent market signals over time

[Page 28]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
28
Concerns with Using “As Is” Conditions for 
Accreditation
•
The ISO considers using “as is” conditions for accreditation inappropriate for the 
following reasons:
–
“as is” condition is typically used for assessing the state of the system's resource adequacy, e.g., 
NPCC and NERC compliance studies
•
Misalignment with market design
–
Breaks the fundamental principle of aligning capacity supply and demand at the reliability criterion
–
Weakens the connection between accreditation outcomes and the reliability standard
–
Applying “as is” conditions for accreditation in isolation would introduce incoherent assumptions 
used for developing other key market parameters, requiring the region to evaluate these differences 
and their effects on market demand and supply parameters, and market prices, for example:
•
Should tie benefits also be calculated assuming “as is” conditions, given that these values impact 
resource accreditation?
•
Would the Net CONE value used to scale the demand curves be calculated assuming the “as is” 
accreditation value while assuming “at criteria” energy and ancillary service revenues?
•
There are likely other assumptions that would need to be assessed as well
•
Distorted investment signals
–
Fails to provide clear signals on the optimal resource mix needed to meet future system needs
–
Results become highly dependent on the assumed resource mix rather than system reliability 
requirements

[Page 29]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
29
Concerns with Using “As Is” Conditions for 
Accreditation (cont.)
•
High volatility and instability 
– Accreditation values could fluctuate significantly under changing system 
conditions
– Outcomes could be driven by short-term or transient system states, rather 
than long-term reliability considerations
•
Methodological and practical challenges
– Accreditation may be driven by a small number of extreme events, leading to 
counterintuitive results
– Calculations become infeasible when the system shows no reliability risk (no 
marginal contribution can be measured)
•
Some administrative risk threshold may be required in this case (e.g., 0.01 days of 
LOLE). However, IA sensitivity results show that accreditation outcomes remain 
similar across the 50/50, 80/20, and 90/10 splits
– Numerical instability arises when the reliability risk is very small, leading to 
unreliable results

[Page 30]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
30
Key Takeaway 
•
To ensure enough capacity to meet the 1-in-10 reliability standard at cost-effective 
rates, the at-criteria framework is utilized consistently in the CAR-SA design to 
reflect this risk tolerance across both ICR and accreditation modeling
–
This aligns reliability outcomes with the market signal
•
Modeling “as is” doesn’t align with the current capacity market design 
•
Accreditation calculated under “as is” conditions may vary significantly from year 
to year
•
When “as is” conditions result in little or no reliability risk, accreditation outcomes 
may become counterintuitive or infeasible to calculate, as the absence of risk does 
not produce the MRI hours needed to measure resource contributions 
•
Additional administrative issues include: 
–
Determining what the “as is” condition means in a continuously changing system 
•
E.g., would this include energy-only resources for capacity modeling, resources on outage, etc., 
at what point in time would “as is” be determined in the process

APPENDIX: NUMERICAL EXAMPLE ON 
MODELING SEVERE WEATHER

[Page 38]

38
Numerical Example: Assumptions
•
Imagine we have two blocks that occur sequentially, b1 and b2
•
In b1, there is equal probability of mild (m) or severe (s) weather
– P(b1 = m) = 0.5
– P(b1 = s) = 0.5
•
In b2, it is again possible to be mild or severe, but we assume that 
this outcome is positively correlated with the temperature in b1
•
In other words, it is more likely to be severe in b2 if it was severe in 
b1 and vice versa
– P(b2 = m | b1 = m) = 0.7
– P(b2 = s | b1 = s) = 0.7

[Page 39]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
39
Numerical Example: Actual Distribution of 
Mild/Severe Blocks
There are four scenarios, where we calculate the probability of 
each while considering that the probabilities associated with b2 
are conditional on the observed weather in b1:
•
P(b1 = m, b2 = m) = 0.35 (=0.5 × 0.7) 
•
P(b1 = m, b2 = s) = 0.15 (=0.5 × 0.3)
•
P(b1 = s, b2 = m) = 0.15 (=0.5 × 0.3)
•
P(b1 = s, b2 = s) = 0.35 (=0.5 × 0.7)
Key observation: The likelihood of severe weather in both 
blocks is 35%

[Page 40]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
40
Numerical Example: Estimated Probabilities 
Ignoring the Cross-Block Correlation
We again calculate the same four probabilities, but no longer consider how 
the weather in b1 impacts the probabilities in b2
•
P(b1 = m) × P(b2 = m) = 0.25 (=0.5 × 0.5) 
•
P(b1 = m) × P(b2 = s) = 0.25 (=0.5 × 0.5)
•
P(b1 = s) × P(b2 = m) = 0.25 (=0.5 × 0.5)
•
P(b1 = s) × P(b2 = s) = 0.25 (=0.5 × 0.5)
Key observation: Ignoring this correlation would lead us to underestimate the 
likelihood of severe weather in both periods (25% when the last slide showed 
it is actually 35%) and instead will tend to overweight events in the middle of 
the distribution (in this case, the likelihood that one block is mild and one is 
severe)

CAR-SA: Updates to Energy Limited and Storage Resource 
Accreditation
WMPP ID:
185
Proposed Effective Date: Q2 2027
• The RAA model is limited in how it utilizes the limited energy 
available from energy limited and storage resources, and does not 
allow such resources to charge other energy storage resources 
during charging constrained hours
• This may lead the modeling process to underestimate the 
reliability contributions of such resources
• The ISO proposes a mechanism that could be used to address this 
limitation via an upward adjustment to the rMRI values of such 
resources made after the RAA modeling process is completed
2

[Page 3]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
BACKGROUND
3

[Page 4]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
4
Background: Energy Limited and Storage Modeling in MARS
• Recall: the RAA model makes a number of assumptions 
regarding the operation of energy limited and energy storage 
resources, including that such resources cannot be used to 
charge energy storage
• In some cases, this could result in the model underestimating 
the resource adequacy contributions of such resources
• For example, in the Near-Term Base Case, a resource with 
1,000 hours of storage and an EFORd of 0 would receive an 
rMRI of 0.85 in the winter and 0.99 in the summer
• A larger reduction in the winter rMRI occurs because it 
includes more charging constrained hours

[Page 5]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
5
Continued ISO Assessment of this Limitation
• As discussed in earlier stakeholder meetings, the ISO has 
assessed potential approaches to address this limitation
• More specifically, the ISO has considered whether there 
are simple design updates that would help address the 
possibility that the GE MARS model understates the 
reliability value of energy limited and storage resources by 
not allowing them to charge storage resources

[Page 6]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
PROPOSED ENERGY LIMITED AND STORAGE 
ACCREDITATION ADJUSTMENT
6

[Page 7]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
7
Adjustment Overview
Potential Energy Limited and Storage Accreditation 
Adjustment Approach:
1. ISO would run the RAA model as discussed in December 
2025 (memo, slides), where resource-level rMRI values 
would be estimated using the perturbation method outlined 
previously
2. After these rMRI values are calculated for all resources, the 
ISO would calculate adjustment values that would be added 
to the rMRI values for energy limited and storage resources

[Page 8]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
8
Accreditation Adjustment Formula
• For resource i, the adjustment would be equal to:
Ai = rMRIi/(1-EFORdi) × (1-max(rMRIu))/max(rMRIu)
• The first term starts with resource i’s model-based rMRI, 
and scales it up to account for its EFORd
• The second term scales the first term so that an energy 
limited resource that performs equivalently to the best 
proxy energy limited resource would receive an 
adjustment just large enough to provide an adjusted rMRI 
of 1

[Page 9]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
9
Impacts of Adjustment
• This adjustment is a simple mechanism by which to account for the 
model’s limitations in reflecting the reliability contributions of energy 
limited and storage resources not being able to charge other energy 
storage resources
• Importantly, for a hypothetical resource with 1,000 hours of storage 
and an EFORd of 0, the adjustment would lead it to receive an rMRI 
value of 1, commensurate with perfect capacity
• Observations about the adjustment:
– Will generally increase as the quantity of charging constrained hours increases, 
meaning it may be larger in the winter (lower max(rMRIu))
– Will be larger for resources with comparatively higher rMRI values (rMRIi)
– Is not expected to affect the accreditation of other resource types

[Page 10]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
10
Impact of Adjustment on Energy Limited and Storage 
Resources for Near-Term Base Case
• Recall: Under the Near-Term Base Case, the fraction of 
charging constrained hours was approximately 15% in the 
winter, and 1% in the summer
• Energy limited/storage resource i would see the following 
adjustment, resulting in a higher rMRI value
– Winter Adjustment: rMRIi/(1-EFORdi) × 0.18
– Summer Adjustment: rMRIi/(1-EFORdi) × 0.01

FirstLight’s revised approach aims to account for two primary factors that do not seem to be addressed by the ISO’s

Assessing the weather impacts of multi

◦Performance obligations will better reflect expected system conditions and resources will

◦Resource adequacy events (capacity scarcity conditions) are more likely to be caused by contingency/transient events

‐ Resource type interactions 
‐ Resource characteristics 
‐ Load shape
‐ Peak load/load scaling 
• Interactions between factors that impact MRI values are complex, particularly when load 
is scaled to a reliability threshold, because scaling LOLE to a specific reliability metric 
has an impact on the nature and timing of MRI events

effects on the simulated events which had largely offsetting impacts (less load scaling 
eliminated some shorter duration events but also decreased the average length events) 
• Forward looking MRI values based on a “at criteria” base case will require a significant 
amount of information from ISO-NE on how expected future conditions will impact the “at 
criteria” case 
◦Forward looking rMRI curves based on expected future market conditions will be 
necessary for investors to have confidence in expected market revenues

Input Assumptions for Offers in All Scenarios

Competitive offer

If a resource’s next best alternative to obtaining a CSO is full participation in the EAS

PPR*BR*H

If a resource’s next best alternative to obtaining a CSO is a temporary exit from all ISO

EAS Costs – EAS Revenues + Going Forward Cost – PPR*(A-BR)*H

Scarcity Hours (H)

informational purposes
•
This presentation also includes sensitivity results for alternative H splits of 25/75 and 75/25
•
The ISO ran 1000 simulations for each scenario with heterogeneous offer inputs and 
calculated average market outcomes (price and quantity) across the simulations

Overview of Simulation Results from the Lower 
Scenario
•
Capacity prices are low under both Current Rules and CAR-SA, reflecting excess supply, low 
assumed H values, and low assumed capital costs incorporated in offer prices
•
Total cost/revenue decreases by $3.1 million (0.35%) under CAR-SA, compared to Current 
Rules, with summer costs somewhat higher than winter costs
–
Capacity prices tend to increase under CAR-SA, but this is offset by a reduction in the quantity 
procured, as the demand curve shifts left, largely reflecting the transition from QC to MRIC, which 
provides greater reliability on a per-MW basis
•
The common value component (PPR*BR*H) increases when going from Current Rules to 
CAR-SA, because PPR and H (with seasonal values summing to the same value as the annual 
H) are constant across the two cases, while BR is higher under CAR-SA due to the QC-to-MRIC 
adjustment
–
For many resources whose MRIC is less than QC, offer prices are higher under CAR-SA when their next 
best alternative is temporary exit, because going forward costs must be recovered over fewer MWs
•
The total clearing quantity tends to be lower under CAR-SA because MRIC tends to be smaller 
than QC for many resources
–
MRIC captures a resource’s estimated performance during simulated hours that are important for 
resource adequacy, while QC is a heuristic metric

Sources of Heterogeneous Offers Across Draws
•
The ISO ran 1000 simulations for each scenario with heterogeneous offer inputs and 
calculated average market outcomes (price and quantity) across the simulations
•
While some components are fixed for a given resource across all simulations, the values for 
capital and fixed costs, risk premiums, and H are stochastically determined and informed by 
resource-specific historical data and predetermined ranges corresponding to the Lower, 
Medium, and Higher scenarios
–
Capital costs exhibit an additional layer of heterogeneity through a probability of cost incurrence: the drawn capital cost 
value from the above is applied to a given resource only with a certain probability, calibrated to reflect the share of 
resources that the ISO observed submitting exit offers in the past
•
Using multiple draws allows the ISO to approximate expected market outcomes under 
uncertainty and to summarize a range of potential outcomes driven by variability in each key 
offer component
•
The graph on the next slide illustrates variability in clearing prices in the Medium scenario 
driven by the heterogeneity in offer components
–
The Medium scenario was chosen for illustration; all scenarios exhibit variability in clearing prices across the 1,000 
simulations, with corresponding graphs provided in the appendix

Overview of the Offer Sensitivity Analysis with H 
Split of 75/25
•
This sensitivity case assumes that 75% of H occurs in the summer and 25% in the 
winter
•
This assumption affects two components
–
Seasonal H values: Although the annual H value remains the same as in the baseline scenarios, 
the seasonal allocation differs
–
Annual BR value: Under the Current Rules, the annual BR value is calculated as an H-weighted 
average of the two seasons; therefore, changes in the seasonal H values will lead to 
corresponding changes in the annual BR value
•
As a result, summer prices are higher than in the baseline across all three 
scenarios (Lower, Medium, Higher), while winter prices are lower than in the 
baseline, reflecting that seasonal offer prices reflect a higher expected H in the 
summer, and a lower expected H in the winter
•
Additional simulation results regarding these cases are included in the appendix

Assigning Firm vs. Non-Firm Quantity in the 
Current Rules Case for Comparison with CAR-SA

We first compute the share of each resource’s total MRIC that is 
considered firm under CAR-SA
•
This share is then applied to the resource’s QC to estimate the 
maximum firm QC MW associated with that resource
•

– Firm QC MWs are assigned first, up to the estimated firm QC limit

Marginal Rate of Substitution between 
Non-Firm Gas and Non-Gas Resources
•
The stylized graph on the next slide illustrates the marginal rate of substitution between non-
firm gas and non-gas resources
•
After clearing the first two supply blocks with the lowest offer prices, the system must choose 
between clearing a non-gas resource and a non-firm gas resource
•
If the system clears the non-gas resource, the system clearing price will be 𝑃𝑃1 and the 
corresponding system clearing quantity will be 𝑄𝑄1
–
The incremental social surplus from this will be zero, since the marginal benefit (the clearing price of 
𝑃𝑃1) is exactly equal to the marginal cost (the offer price of the resource at 𝑃𝑃1)
–
However, the incremental social surplus from clearing the non-firm gas resource instead at 𝑄𝑄1 is 
(𝑃𝑃1−𝑃𝑃2) plus a gas price that is bounded by −(𝑃𝑃2 −𝑃𝑃3), totaling a net benefit with a lower bound of 
(𝑃𝑃1−𝑃𝑃3) −(𝑃𝑃2 −𝑃𝑃3) = 𝑃𝑃1 −𝑃𝑃2, which is positive
•
Because clearing the non-firm gas resource yields a higher marginal net benefit, the system 
selects it as the third supply block
–
The system clearing price is set at 𝑃𝑃2 and the corresponding system clearing quantity will be 𝑄𝑄2
–
Note that the gas price in this case is exactly equal to the negative value of the clearing price of 
(𝑃𝑃2−𝑃𝑃3), making the marginal net benefit of clearing the non-firm gas supply block at 𝑄𝑄2 equal zero

AMBIENT AIR PROCESS
3

[Page 4]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
4
Ambient Air Process
•
The capability of thermal generators generally declines at high 
temperatures 
•
The Forward Capacity Market (FCM) and CAR-PD 
included provisions allowing the Lead Market Participant (LMP) 
of a thermal generator to offer Ambient Air MWs above the 
Capacity Offer Price Threshold (COPT) without cost justification
•
Ambient Air MWs equal the difference between a resource’s 
Qualified Capacity (QC) at 90°F and rating at 100°F 
– The ISO verifies this reduction based on physical limit documentation 
submitted by the LMP

[Page 5]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
5
Ambient Air: CAR-SA Treatment
• LMPs may continue to offer Ambient Air MWs above the 
COPT without cost justification by submitting 
documentation of Ambient Air MWs in their Qualification 
Data Submission Package

[Page 6]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
6
CAR-SA Ambient Air Calculation
• To quantify Ambient Air MWs in MRIC, Ambient Air MWs 
will equal:
 
 
max[rMRI x (MCap – rating at 100°F), 0]
• We will walk through two examples to demonstrate how 
this formula works

[Page 7]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
7
Quantifying Ambient Air MWs in MRIC
• Example 1:
– Resource with Maximum Capability (MCap) > rating at 100°F 
• Consider a unit with the following characteristics:
– 90°F rating: 500 MW
– 100°F rating: 475 MW
– MCap: 490 MW
• Ambient Air MWs = max [rMRI x (490-475),0], a positive 
value because the resource’s MCap exceeds its rating at 
100°F so the difference can be offered above the COPT

[Page 8]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
8
Quantifying Ambient Air MWs in MRIC
• Example 2: 
– Resource with MCap < rating at 100°F 
• Consider a unit with the following characteristics:
– 90°F rating: 500 MW
– 100°F rating: 475 MW
– MCap: 465 MW
• Ambient Air MWs = max [rMRI x (465-475),0] = 0
• This resource is not eligible to offer Ambient Air MWs 
because its MCap is already below its rating at 100°F

Unexpected Full Forced Outage
•
As discussed last month, the ISO introduced the unexpected full 
forced outage concept at the May MC
– Mechanism to address concerns regarding an unexpected full, forced outage 
after the cost workbook submission deadline for supplier-side market power, 
and before the seasonal auction offer submittal window
•
Stakeholders expressed interest in the ISO providing additional 
procedural detail on the concept
•
Next, the ISO will discuss:
– Trading opportunities under FCM, CAR-PD, and CAR-SA, and where the 
unexpected full forced outage concept fits within the CAR-SA process
– The unexpected full forced outage qualification process
•
Specifics on submittal and review of an unexpected full forced outage
•
Limitations on the qualification and application of an unexpected full Forced Outage

[Page 14]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
14
Background: FCM & CAR-PD Trading Opportunities
•
Under FCM, the following trading opportunities exist just before and during the annual CCP:
–
In ARA3, resources can seek to shed CSO via a demand bid
•
Effective for the annual CCP
–
After ARA3, and throughout the annual CCP, resources can seek to shed CSO in the monthly events
•
Under CAR-PD, the following mechanisms and trading opportunities exist just before, and 
during the annual CCP
–
Before supplier-side market power cost workbook deadline, if resource costs are higher than the 
COPT, a participant may submit a Proposed Capacity Offer and cost workbook to the IMM
•
May include cost associated with an outage
–
Then submit an offer into the primary auction reflective of costs, subject to mitigation
•
Effective for the annual CCP
–
After supplier-side market power cost workbook deadline
•
Submit an offer in the primary auction reflective of costs, up to the COPT
–
Effective for the annual CCP
•
After primary auction & throughout annual CCP, resources can seek to shed in the monthly events

[Page 15]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
15
Background: CAR-SA Trading Opportunities
•
Under CAR-SA, the following mechanisms and trading opportunities 
exist just before and during the season
– Before supplier-side market power cost workbook deadline, if resource costs 
are higher than the COPT, a participant may submit a Proposed Capacity Offer 
and cost workbook to the IMM
•
May include cost associated with an outage
– Then submit an offer in the seasonal auction reflective of costs, subject to mitigation
•
Effective for the six-month season
– After supplier-side market power cost workbook deadline
•
Enter an unexpected full forced outage 
– Effective for the six-month season
-or-
•
Submit an offer in the seasonal auction reflective of costs, up to the COPT
– Effective for the six-month season
•
After the seasonal auction and throughout the season, seek to shed in monthly 
events

[Page 16]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
16
Unexpected Full Forced Outage Qualification 
Process
•
If a resource unexpectedly becomes fully unavailable for an entire 
season, a participant may request to remove the resource capacity 
from the seasonal auction using the unexpected full forced outage 
provision
– This is a provision in addition to the available trading opportunities to 
manage CSO
•
The unexpected full forced outage provision will have the following 
criteria:
– The resource is on a forced outage, which occurred at any time
•
Based on stakeholder feedback, the requirement to consider only outages submitted into CROW (Control Room 
Operations Window) after the supplier-side market power cost workbook deadline is no longer applicable
– The resource is on a full outage
– The outage duration covers the entire season

[Page 17]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
17
Unexpected Full Forced Outage Qualification 
Process
•
Procedurally, during an unexpected full forced outage window (~1 week 
before the seasonal auction offer submittal window opens):
– Submit request via AskISO
•
Provide resource information & CROW outage(s)
•
Request is binding
•
ISO & IMM will review the request, verify assets, resources, and outage(s)
– If approved, the resource MRIC will be reduced to 0
•
Additionally, if approved, the resource cannot acquire a CSO in the monthly events 
within the season
– At the May MC it was discussed that a resource could acquire a CSO in the monthly 
events if the outage were subsequently revised to end prior to the end of the season
•
Additionally, a resource can submit both a Proposed Capacity Offer 
and cost workbook, and then submit an unexpected full forced 
outage request

[Page 18]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
18
Unexpected Full Forced Outage Qualification 
Process
•
At the May MC, stakeholders expressed interest in applying the 
unexpected full forced outage concept to i) planned outages,
ii) resources which are on a partial outage, iii) resources which 
are fully out of service for a portion of the season, and 
iv) resources that are out of service due to transmission
– For each of these conditions, the Proposed Capacity Offer and cost 
workbook submittal process, in conjunction with trading 
opportunities, allows for managing CSO for the portion of the 
resource’s availability
• For resources out of service due to transmission, if the transmission 
outage is forced or an emergency, causing a full, forced outage of the 
resource for the duration of the season, then the resource would be eligible 
for an unexpected full forced outage

[Page 2]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
2
Non-firm Gas Capacity Demand Curve
WMPP ID: 185
Proposed Effective Date: Q2 2027
•
During the winter, the quantity of gas available for power generation is limited
•
This regional gas supply constraint impacts gas resources’ ability to contribute to 
resource adequacy in the winter
•
As part of the Capacity Auction Reforms (CAR), the impact of the regional gas 
constraint will be reflected in gas capacity market compensation through a 
non-firm gas capacity demand curve
•
This novel design represents a significant improvement relative to current rules, 
where the regional gas constraint is not reflected in the capacity market
•
Today’s material covers the following topics:
– Proposal to not adjust the gas demand curve in response to firm gas contracts
– Follow up on the firm gas contract requirements discussion at the April MC
– CSO bilateral transactions and the non-firm gas constraint
2

[Page 3]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
3
ISO and Analysis Group to Continue Work on Gas Design
• Today’s discussion reflects the ISO’s current thinking, and we welcome 
stakeholder feedback as we move to finalize the design in the coming months
• The ISO plans to assess potential enhancements to these proposals in the 
months to come and after the CAR-SA filing

[Page 4]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
FIRM CONTRACTS WILL NOT ADJUST 
THE GAS DEMAND CURVE
4

[Page 5]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
5
CAR-SA Gas Demand Curve Represents Novel but 
Complex Design Element
• Reflecting the reliability impact of the regional gas constraint on capacity 
market compensation through a gas demand curve represents one of the more 
novel but complex elements of the CAR-SA proposal
• Challenges include:
– Determining the requirements for a gas contract to be considered “firm”
– Determining the reliability contribution of those firm contracts
• This necessarily includes estimating the extent to which contracts provide “incremental gas”
—gas that would not have been available for power generation in the absence of the contract— 
during tight system conditions when resource adequacy is at risk
– Incorporating the gas constraint into auction clearing
• More difficult than locational constraints, as resources can be behind both a locational constraint 
and a gas constraint, and the same resource can be behind separate constraints (e.g., a resource 
in an export-constrained zone that has both firm and non-firm MRI Capacity)
• Additionally, depending on firm arrangements, resources could be subject to the constraint in one 
auction but not the next

[Page 6]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
6
Gas Demand Curve Adjustment Can Distort Market 
Outcomes
• In May, Analysis Group (AG) proposed that the gas demand curve be shifted in 
response to firm arrangements made by non-firm gas resources
• Implicit in this approach is an assumption that all MWs that are designated in 
advance as firm clear the market 
• If this assumption does not hold, then the shifted gas demand curve may not 
consider all gas available for power generation when determining capacity 
awards, which could:
1.

ANALYSIS GROUP, INC. 
This memorandum outlines proposed specifications and requirements for gas-only natural gas 
resources opting to designate as “firm” resources (“Firm Capacity”) that are not subject to the 
gas constraint within the Capacity Auction Reform (“CAR”) process.  This memorandum 
updates specifications and requirements originally posted on April 15, 2026 given further 
research and information, including feedback and comments received from stakeholders.1  The 
proposed design is not static, and may evolve further over time in response to additional 
feedback, and after its initial implementation in CCP 19.    
I. 
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
The ISO-NE region faces a system-wide gas infrastructure constraint that potentially increases 
resource adequacy risk in the winter months due to limits on the delivery of natural gas to gas-
only resources.  The Firm Capacity specifications and requirements outlined in this 
memorandum are intended to (1) provide compensation to gas-only resources commensurate 
with resource adequacy benefit they provide to the region and (2) encourage cost-effective 
actions by gas-only generators to mitigate the gas infrastructure constraint. 
In sum, resources electing as Firm Capacity will need to maintain fuel supply arrangements that 
meet certain specifications.  The required specifications will differ for arrangements by pipeline 
and by LNG terminal, as described below: 
• Pipeline 
o Firm Capacity requires firm pipeline transportation (primary or in-path secondary 
firm) in amounts sufficient to sustain operations for 16 hours on each day at 
elected capacity for the three-month Winter Contract Period (December to 
February).  No-notice firm service is not required. 
o Firm transportation service is required to have a receipt point outside New 
England that meets certain locational requirements specific to each of the 
pipelines delivering into New England. 
o Firm Capacity does not need to specify particular supply arrangements.  
o Generators can opt to contract with marketers for gas supply if the marketer 
selling the gas supply demonstrates that the supply is backed by firm 
transportation rights in line with the requirements and specifications in this 
document. We propose that generators must supply an affidavit from an officer of 
the marketer company attesting that the firmness of its contract is consistent with 
the Firm Capacity requirements.  
 
1 The initial proposal was communicated through posted materials and a stakeholder presentation to the NEPOOL 
Markets Committee on April 15, 2026.  Posted materials include: 2026-04-14-16 MC/RC 7.c - CAR-SA: Gas-Only 
Resource Contract Requirements – Memo (Link), and 2026-04-14-16 MC/RC 7.c - CAR-SA: Gas-Only Resource 
Contract Requirements – Presentation (Link).

[Page 3]
Page 3 of 18 
 
 
 
 
ANALYSIS GROUP, INC. 
o On each electric day, market participants should maintain firm transportation to 
support offers into the day-ahead markets and fulfillment of must-offer 
requirements.  After day-ahead market clearing, market participants can release 
firm transportation to the market not needed to meet expected energy supplies.   
• LNG Terminal 
o Firm Capacity requires, at minimum, a peaking contract with an LNG terminal 
(e.g., Saint John LNG, Everett Marine Terminal, Northeast Gateway) for 20 days 
with a Maximum Daily Quantity (“MDQ”) sufficient to sustain operation of 
elected capacity for 16 hours per day.   
o Firm Capacity electing through an LNG terminal arrangement does not need to 
specify particular transportation arrangements to deliver supplies to a particular 
facility. 
• For both types of arrangements, market participants will be provided flexibility in the use 
of the procured services.  When using pipeline resources, market participants can market 
procured services if not needed to fulfill day-ahead cleared positions.  When using LNG 
terminal services, there are no specifications on use.  
• For either type of arrangement, market participants should maintain the arrangements for 
the duration of the Winter Contract Period, subject to certain exceptions.   
• The remainder of this document discusses these specifications in further detail.  
II. 
FIRM CAPACITY SPECIFICATIONS AND REQUIREMENTS 
A. 
Winter Contract Period 
A resource electing as Firm Capacity must meet the required specifications for a three-
month winter contract period, including December, January and February (“Winter 
Contract Period”).  This period captures most of the resource adequacy risk from ISO-NE 
modeling, includes most of the historical periods of tight natural gas conditions, and aligns with 
the modeled winter period in the AG gas availability model.  In principle, a shorter or longer 
Winter Contract Period could be specified, potentially reflecting measures of gas system 
constraint risks under particular system conditions.  However, the three-month period 
appropriately identifies a reasonable period of time, particularly given the potential for risks to 
shift within the winter period in the future.  
B. 
Product Specifications 
Due to the infrastructure differences in the supply and delivery dynamics for pipeline gas versus 
LNG terminals in New England, we specify different Firm Capacity specifications for gas 
service from each source.

[Page 4]
Page 4 of 18 
 
 
 
 
ANALYSIS GROUP, INC. 
1. Pipeline Gas 
ISO-NE is served primarily by five major interstate pipelines, with the tariff for each pipeline 
defining its firm service rate classes: Algonquin Gas Pipeline (“Algonquin”),2 Iroquois Gas 
Transmission System (“Iroquois”),3 Tennessee Gas Pipeline (“TGP” or “Tennessee”),4 
Maritimes & Northeast (“M&N”),5 and Portland Natural Gas Transmission System (“PNGTS”).6  
The specifications described in this section, in principle, apply to all five pipelines, except as 
noted below. 
Resources relying on pipeline gas for Firm Capacity must secure firm gas transportation 
rights for every day in the three-month Winter Contract Period in a quantity sufficient to 
power the elected Firm Capacity for 16 hours per day.  The 16-hour requirement is consistent 
with the proposed accreditation of energy-limited resources, based on GE MARS modeling.7  In 
practice, the most likely way for generators to secure firm gas transportation rights on peak 
demand days is to contract for firm transportation service in advance of the Winter Contract 
Period for the full Winter Contract Period.  Arrangements that only provide service “when 
needed” are not, to our knowledge, currently available.  Peak days for gas demand are not known 
in advance of the winter and contracts to support firm delivery only during the relevant market 
conditions are not currently available (and could be challenging to structure).  Thus, Firm 
Capacity resources relying on firm transportation pipeline gas contracts must have service for all 
days in the Winter Contract Period. 
This requirement precludes the reliance on short-term firm transportation rights released within 
the winter (e.g., daily) by shippers that do not need all rights to serve customer needs.  Local 
distribution companies (“LDCs”), in particular, hold the majority of the firm pipeline rights in 
the region and typically make unused supplies available to the market through, for example, 
marketers managing their transportation contracts under Asset Management Agreements 
 
2 In the Algonquin tariff, AFT-1 is Firm Transportation Service, and AFT-E is No-Notice Firm Transportation 
Service. Algonquin Gas Transmission, LLC, Sixth Revised Volume No. 1, available at 
https://infopost.enbridge.com/infopost/AGHome.asp?Pipe=AG. 
3 In the Iroquois tariff, RTS is Firm Reserved Transportation Service. FERC Gas Tariff, Second Revised Volume 
No. 1 of Iroquois Gas Transmission System, L.P., July 24, 2025, available at 
https://ioly.iroquois.com/infopost/#entiretariff.  
4 In the Tennessee tariff, FT-A is Firm Transportation, and FT-PS is No-Notice Firm Transportation (PowerServe, 
optional no-notice service component). FERC NGA Gas Tariff, Sixth Revised Volume No. 1 of Tennessee Gas 
Pipeline Company, L.L.C., Docket No. RP23-863-001, June 30, 2023, available at 
https://pipeline2.kindermorgan.com/Tariff/SubIndex.aspx?category=RATESCHED&code=TGP. 
5 In the Maritimes & Northeast pipeline tariff, there are five firm transportation rate schedules: 365 day firm 
transportation service (MN365), 151 day firm transportation service (MN151), 90 day firm transportation service 
(MN90), off-peak firm transportation service (MNOP), and firm transportation service on lateral line (MNLFT). 
FERC Gas Tariff, First Revised Volume No. 1 of Maritimes & Northeast Pipeline, L.L.C., Docket No. RP04-189-
000, available at https://www.ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2020-05/029524_000100__contents.pdf.  
6 In the Portland Natural Gas Transmission System, FT is Firm Transportation, and HRS is Hourly Reserve [firm] 
Service. FERC Gas Tariff, Second Revised Volume No. 1, Portland Natural Gas Transmission System, Docket No. 
RP06-449-000, available at https://www.ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2020-05/015544_000100__contents.pdf. 
7 See ISO’s June 2026 materials on updates to energy limited and energy storage accreditation.

[Page 5]
Page 5 of 18 
 
 
 
 
ANALYSIS GROUP, INC. 
(“AMAs”).  Use of this type of service that is contingent on LDC release does not secure rights 
to pipeline capability in advance of the winter, but transfers rights previously secured by another 
entity.  Under an AMA, LDCs retain their right to use firm transportation rights when needed, 
including periods of high customer demand in the winter.  As a result, ISO-NE cannot be 
confident that generators relying on these types of arrangements will have access to fuel during 
the tight gas market conditions that are important for resource adequacy.  Thus, this type of 
service is not “firm.” 
Additional specifications regarding the type, required quantity, and receipt and delivery points 
for firm transportation service are provided below.   
Market participants electing Firm Capacity will not be required to demonstrate any supply 
arrangements.  While supply requirements could, in principle, further insulate resources from 
the system-wide gas constraint, our current assessment of the tradeoffs associated with requiring 
particular supply arrangements is that the benefits of requiring such arrangements do not 
outweigh the costs.  There are two primary rationales for this decision.  First, with respect to 
pipeline-supplied gas, the primary source of resource adequacy risk due to the winter gas 
constraint is the limitation of pipeline resources rather than a limitation on supplies at receipt 
points.  Second, there are a wide range of potential supply arrangements, with varying levels of 
associated reliability, that are currently used by market participants.  Requiring that market 
participants utilize certain supply arrangements may thus constrain market participants’ fuel 
procurement strategies.     
(a) Required Type of Firm Transportation Service  
Resources will be required to hold primary firm pipeline transportation rights, under 
which they can use either primary or in-path secondary nominations.  
FERC defines firm gas transportation service on interstate pipelines as the following: “Service 
on a firm basis means that the service is not subject to a prior claim by another customer or 
another class of service […].”8  Primary firm service is the most reliable form of gas 
transportation service.  With primary firm, the shipper can typically ship gas supplies, 
particularly when nominated in the first of multiple daily nomination cycles.  The industry 
standard North American Energy Standards Board (“NAESB”) nomination schedule includes 
five daily nomination cycles, with the first being the timely nomination (day-ahead, nominations 
due by 1pm central clock time (“CCT”)).9  Per FERC: “In scheduling service, nominations of 
 
8 18 CFR 284.7, Firm transportation service, available at https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-18/chapter-I/subchapter-
I/part-284. 
9 151 FERC ¶ 61,049, Coordination of the Scheduling Processes of Interstate Natural Gas Pipelines and Public 
Utilities, Final Rule, Docket No. RM14-2-000, Order No. 809, April 16, 2015, pp. 61, 68-69, available at 
https://www.ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2020-08/M-1.pdf.  Other nominations include: evening (day-ahead, due by 
6pm CCT), and Intraday 1-3 (three additional nomination cycles throughout the gas delivery day, with nominations 
due at 10am, 2:30pm and 7pm CCT).  CCT is the prevailing Central Time Zone time throughout the year, 
accounting for daylight savings where applicable.

[Page 6]
Page 6 of 18 
 
 
 
 
ANALYSIS GROUP, INC. 
primary firm service enjoy the highest priority, followed by nominations of secondary firm 
service, and then interruptible service as the lowest priority.”10     
Primary firm nominations are for gas transported from the primary receipt point to the primary 
delivery point in a given contract.11  Primary firm service also entitles the holder to nominate 
shipments for receipt and delivery to points in the same pipeline rate zones as the contract 
primary receipt and delivery points.12  Thus, primary firm service can be used for nominations to 
“secondary” points as well as the contract’s “primary” receipt and primary delivery points. This 
is referred to as “secondary firm service.”  While secondary firm service has a lower priority in 
scheduling nominations than primary firm service, secondary service, particularly when in-path, 
represents service offered by dedicated portions of pipeline capacity.  Moreover, once scheduled, 
secondary nominations cannot be “bumped” for any other customers seeking to ship gas, 
including those nominating from primary receipt or delivery points.   Secondary nominations 
thus offer important flexibility in the use of primary firm service to ensure efficient use of the 
gas transportation system and to maintain liquidity of gas transportation supplies to help meet all 
customer needs. 
Secondary firm nominations can be “in-path” or “out-of-path.”  In this context, the “path” refers

delivery, or both points are outside of the primary receipt/delivery point contract path.  
Secondary out-of-path nominations have a lower scheduling priority and are more likely to be

Receipt and Delivery Point Rationale: 
 
The choice of required receipt and delivery point requirements aims to ensure service that allows 
the resource to avoid being subject to the New England system-wide physical infrastructure 
constraint that limits the quantity of gas that can flow into the region.  Thus, the requirements are 
designed to facilitate flow of gas into the region, but not necessarily delivery to specific plants.  
The required delivery point is chosen to ensure that gas supplies reasonably reach into the gas 
system, but do not require mitigation of potential constraints along laterals, which reflect facility-
specific supply risks.  
 
The required receipt points reflect a point that mitigates gas delivery constraints into the New 
England region.  In many cases, required receipt points are points in close proximity to the New 
England geographic border.  In some cases, notably PNGTS, the requirement accounts for 
certain out-of-region constraints that may be the limiting factor on supplies into the region.  In 
some cases, these requirements align with the contract path of supplies in LDC supply plans.19  
In other cases, these requirements are less stringent than those in LDC supply plans.20  While 
less stringent in some cases, our proposed receipt points are nonetheless reasonable because the 
delivery constraints getting gas into New England are generally more severe than those faced 
when traversing other regions (e.g., New York State).  Our choice of receipt points also 
simplifies the process of specifying eligible receipt points given the wide array of transportation 
paths that could plausibly deliver supply from more-distant locations with physically liquid 
supplies (e.g., Marcellus) to New England.  Further, our choice of receipt points may increase the 
volume and lower the cost of required transportation services, thus likely striking a better 
balance between cost and benefits in setting the receipt point requirement.  While we do not 
propose that all receipt points originate at locations with physically liquid supply at this time, we 
expect that ISO New England may review these decisions after future auctions to ensure that

(c) Contracts with Marketers for Pipeline Supply 
Instead of contracting directly with pipeline operators for firm transportation, resources also have 
the option to contract with marketers for pipeline gas supply to qualify as Firm Capacity.  
Marketer pipeline gas supply contracts must meet the following requirements.   
First, the underlying arrangements used by the marketer to deliver supplies under the contract 
must be consistent with the specification of pipeline Firm Capacity in this document.  To fulfill 
this requirement, the marketer counterparty must demonstrate that it holds primary or secondary 
firm transportation contractual rights sufficient to service its contract with the generation 
resource.  Such demonstration should include specific firm transportation contracts used to 
support the proposed service or other materials identifying particular firm transportation 
contracts used to support the proposed service. These firm transportation contractual rights must 
be consistent with the firm transportation specifications in this document and should not include 
any short-term or recallable capacity release firm transportation.  When a market participant opts 
to contract for pipeline gas supply through a marketer, these requirements are necessary to 
ensure the resource’s gas supply is supported by firm pipeline transportation.  
Second, we propose that generators must supply an affidavit from an officer of the marketer 
company attesting that the fact that the firm pipeline transportation used by the market 
participant to designate its resource as Firm Capacity (1) be used to supply service for the 
designated resource consistent with the specifications and requirements for firm pipeline 
transportation outlined in this document, and (2) will not be used to provide gas supply service to 
other customers in a manner that is inconsistent with the specifications and requirements outlined 
in this document, including such service to resources designating as Firm Capacity.  
2. LNG 
Market participants electing resources as Firm Capacity can choose to enter into a contract with 
one of the region’s LNG terminals, including Everett Marine Terminal (“EMT”), Northeast 
Gateway, and Saint John LNG. 
Below, we describe the specifications for Firm Capacity for market participants choosing to elect 
Firm Capacity under an LNG contract. 
(a) Requirements for Firm Service 
To qualify as Firm Capacity, LNG contracts should be executed directly with an LNG 
terminal operator and must, at minimum, provide sufficient flexibility regarding notice 
and nomination to (1) allow the market participant to receive supplies when nominated by 
a deadline no earlier than 9 a.m. ET on the business day before delivery and (2) allow the 
market participant to modify its initial nomination (subject to the MDQ) if modifications 
can be effectuated by the pipeline transporters.

(b) Contract Duration and Volume Requirements 
Resources electing as Firm Capacity will be required to procure gas supply through an 
LNG contract for a minimum duration of 20 days during the Winter Contract Period with 
an MDQ sufficient to sustain full operations of elected capacity for 16 hours per day.  We 
refer to this as a “peaking contract”.  We have determined that such a contract provides a 
sufficient amount of LNG supply to run Firm Capacity when needed to mitigate gas system 
constraint risks.    
A peaking contract requires certain contract terms, including a MDQ and a total contract 
quantity (“TCQ”). 22  The contract’s duration is calculated by dividing the TCQ by the MDQ.  
For each of the 20 days of the contract supply, the MDQ must be sufficient to sustain continuous 
operations of elected Firm Capacity for 16 hours.

with a fixed reservation charge for supplies reserved and a commodity charge to release supplies.

December, January and February as of the first business day of August prior to the 
relevant winter and

C. 
Requirements About Firm Service Use 
A market-driven approach to specifying rules about generator firm gas use and sale of firm gas 
rights will ensure that the liquidity of the gas market is not overly restricted by any Firm 
Capacity contract use requirements, while also ensuring that the firm service secured by Firm 
Capacity resources supports reliability.   
To maintain liquidity, resources relying on pipeline services will be permitted to sell their firm 
gas supply and transportation rights within the Winter Contract Period, while still maintaining 
their Firm Capacity designation.  In theory, once firm gas transportation is committed to the ISO-
NE market, it would be suboptimal to constrain who is using this service.  The generator that 
contracted for the firm gas still deserves to be compensated differently than non-firm generators 
because, but-for that firm contract, the firm gas supply may not have otherwise been available to 
the ISO-NE system as a whole.

D. 
Requirements for Maintaining Service 
All counterparties to firm gas transportation and supply contracts submitted by a resource to 
qualify as Firm Capacity must maintain those contracts for the entire Winter Contract Period, 
unless requesting an exemption due to relevant circumstances (e.g., extended facility outage).   
E. 
Firm Fuel MW Elections 
Resources will elect a quantity of MWs to be designated as Firm Capacity (“elected MWs”), 
where the maximum quantity a resource can elect is its marginal reliability impact (“MRI”) 
Capacity.  Elected MWs will reflect the type of firm gas service used to support the election and 
corresponding calculations to determine elected MWs given contract details and the generator’s 
assumed heat rate28 to align the volume of fuel procured with the corresponding elected MWs.   
While Firm Capacity elections are capped at MRI capacity, fuel contracts must be in terms of 
physical capability.  For example, a gas-only resource with 80 MW of MRI capacity, 100 MW of 
physical capability, and a 7.0 MMBtu/MWh heat rate would require firm transportation for 10.8 
MMcf per day for the entire Winter Contract Period if electing all 80 MW of MRI capacity under 
pipeline supply, where this quantity is calculated as:  
10.8 MMcf = 100 MW x 7.0 MMBtu/MWh x 16 hours x 0.001 MMcf/MMBtu.29

an MDQ of 10.8 MMcf, calculated as above, and a TCQ of 216 MMcf (20 * 10.8 MMcf).    
Resources may submit partial Firm Capacity elections that do not reflect their entire MRI 
capacity (i.e., some quantity of MWs less than the plant’s full MRI capacity).  Following the 
above numerical example, if the resource with 80 MW of MRI capacity and 100 MW physical 
capability wants to submit half of its MRI capacity as Firm Capacity (40 MW), it would need to 
contract for fuel for half of its physical capability (50 MW), where the quantity is calculated as 
5.4 MMcf under pipeline supply, and 108 MMcf under LNG supply (20 * 5.4 MMcf). 
Partial Firm Capacity elections maximize the potential firm gas that can be contracted.  For 
example, in the event a generator can only procure firm gas that meets the Firm Capacity 
contract specification criteria for part of its capacity, it is more optimal for overall reliability and 
economic efficiency to allow that generator to procure partial firm gas, rather than forcing the 
entire plant to remain non-firm by default.

Market participants designating a gas-only resource as Firm Capacity must provide the following 
information to ISO-NE:

specifications for pipeline or LNG supply, as described above, including pipeline 
operator firm transportation contracts and LNG terminal supply contracts.  If relying on 
marketer supply supported by firm pipeline transportation, the marketer must provide 
contracts (and other relevant materials) that demonstrate that it has firm transportation 
contracts that meet the relevant specifications, including an affidavit from an officer of 
the marketing company, as specified above.  
• A signed affidavit from an officer of the participant’s company stating that the submitted 
contracts and documentation meet the requirements for a firm contract as set forth in the 
tariff and corresponding market manuals.

•
The ISO will cap the Capacity Balancing Ratio (BR) at 1.0 for compliance 
with the FERC order in Docket EL25-106, issued in response to NEPGA’s 
Section 206 filing about the Pay-for-Performance (PFP) design 
–
Proposed effective date is October 1, 2026
•
Changes to the accreditation framework under CAR-SA may impact 
the frequency at which the BR reaches and is capped at 1.0, 
potentially reducing PFP payments to overperformers
•
Stakeholders requested consideration of the BR calculation 
and cap under CAR-SA 
•
Today’s discussion:
–
Introduces the topic of BR capping under CAR-SA
–
Introduces conforming changes to annual stop loss for a seasonal market

[Page 3]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
BACKGROUND
Balancing Ratio, Commission order, and interactions 
with CAR-SA
3

[Page 4]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
4
Background
•
Under PFP, the Balancing Ratio (BR) is used to determine a capacity 
resource’s share-of-system obligation during Capacity Scarcity 
Conditions (CSC)
– A resource’s Capacity Performance Score and Capacity Performance Payment 
(CPP) are determined by its performance relative to its obligation
•
The BR is calculated for each five-minute CSC interval as: 
BR = (Load + Reserve Requirement) / Total Capacity Supply Obligation 
•
Resources have historically been credited or charged for performance 
deviations at the same fixed Performance Payment Rate (PPR, $/MWh)
•
CPPs are structured as transfers among under- and over-performing 
resources

[Page 5]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
5
Commission Order and Compliance Changes
•
In January 2026, FERC granted the NEPGA complaint in part and ordered the BR 
capped at 1.0 
–
A BR cap at 1.0 ensures capacity resources are not charged for failing to perform beyond their 
CSO MW during scarcity conditions
•
Since CPPs are a transfer among resources, capping the BR can result in a 
deficiency of charges collected to fund payments to overperformers
–
The ISO’s compliance proposal (March MC) will reduce payments for overperformance when a 
deficiency of CPPs exists
•
FERC cited the ISO’s current capacity market accreditation method in its 
determination
–
The current framework accredits most resource types near their maximum physical capability, 
called Qualified Capacity (QC)
–
When the BR exceeds 1.0, many capacity resources are not capable of physically producing 
their pro rata share of system needs
•
FERC also acknowledged the importance of providing strong incentives for 
resources to perform during CSCs

[Page 6]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
6
Balancing Ratio Cap Interactions with CAR-SA
•
With the change to a Marginal Reliability Impact (MRI) accreditation framework 
under CAR-SA, resource accreditation will be based on expected performance 
during simulated hours when resource adequacy is at risk
–
In total across the NE system, resources’ MRI Capacity (MRIC) values are lower than 
QC values (March MC Resource Accreditation Modeling Impact Analysis)
•
Stakeholders have raised concerns that the change to MRI-based 
accreditation will produce higher BRs, which could lead to more instances of 
the BR being capped at 1.0
–
Measurement of load + reserve requirement in numerator is unchanged
–
Decrease in total CSO in denominator -> increase in BRs
•
Higher BRs and more frequent BR capping will lead to a larger deficiency of 
CPPs and larger reductions in the “effective” PPR for overperformance
–
A BR of 1.15 that is capped at 1.0 will produce a larger deficiency of CPPs than a BR 
of 1.05 that is capped at 1.0

[Page 7]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
DESIGN OPTIONS
Options for the Balancing Ratio under CAR-SA
7

[Page 8]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
Design Objectives 
8
•
Simple and implementable
•
Complies with the logic outlined in the NEPGA complaint and 
FERC order
•
Sound market design, including
– Strong performance incentives for overperformers
– Equitable settlement outcomes across resources 
•
These objectives are in tension! 
•
Next: Discuss three conceptual approaches to BR capping 
under CAR-SA

[Page 9]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
9
Approach 1: Cap the Balancing Ratio at 1.0
•
Continuing to cap the BR at 1.0 requires no changes from current 
proposal
•
Ensures no resources have an obligation above their maximum 
physical capability
– Complies with NEPGA complaint and FERC order
•
Does not maintain as strong performance incentives for 
overperformers under CAR-SA
– Capping may occur more frequently
– A BR capped at 1.0 results in less underperformance and more 
overperformance relative to an uncapped BR
– May lead to significant reductions in the “effective” PPR for overperformance

[Page 10]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
10
Approach 2: Remove Cap on the Balancing Ratio 
•
Remove cap on BR, reverting to rules that were in place prior to the 
NEPGA complaint and FERC order
– FERC order cited current accreditation method as the primary reason for 
requiring the cap since many resources are accredited near or at their 
maximum physical output
– With MRI-based accreditation, resources will generally be accredited below 
their maximum physical output 
•
Does not prevent resources from being held to an obligation beyond 
their physical capability
– When selling capacity, resources accept a share-of-system financial obligation 
•
Ensures overperformers receive the full payment rate
– Payment rate known in advance
– Payment rate equal to the charge rate

[Page 11]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
11
Approach 3: Modified Cap on the Balancing Ratio 
•
Cap the BR above 1.0, at a level tied to the total physical capability associated with 
the amount of capacity sold
•

Conforming changes to annual stop loss in CAR-SA
