Stop-Loss Limits Under CAR-SA
• As the ISO noted during the CAR scoping discussions in 
2024, it does not intend to propose material changes to 
PFP under CAR
– August 2024 MC
• However, some conforming changes are likely necessary
• Next: Provide background on the PFP stop-loss 
mechanism, and propose a narrow change to reflect the 
introduction of a seasonal market

[Page 16]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
16
Background: Stop Loss Under Current Rules
• Two stop-loss mechanisms were included as part of the 
PFP design that was approved in 2014
• Monthly Stop Loss: Places a cap on a resource’s 
monthly PFP charges for underperformance equal to the 
maximum auction clearing price (in $/kw-m)
• Annual Stop Loss: Caps annual losses that a resource 
can incur across the annual CCP equal to three times its 
maximum monthly potential net loss

[Page 17]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
17
Rationale Behind Inclusion of Stop-Loss Limits
•
The stop-loss limits are mutual insurance mechanisms that cap a resource’s 
exposure due to underperformance while maintaining strong performance 
incentives
•
A limit prevents unlimited financial liability by placing a predictable, calculable 
cap on the amount a resource can lose due to non-performance during a CSC
•
Capping charges for a non-performing resource can create a funding shortfall, 
which is covered by other capacity suppliers with CSOs in the market
–
This creates a system analogous to a mutual insurance pool, where the collective 
group of suppliers covers the excessive losses of a peer
–
The design also buffers consumers from paying for a funding shortfall
•
Some resources reached the monthly stop-loss limits during the CSC event on 
June 24, 2025, but there have been no instances where annual stop-loss limits 
have been reached

[Page 18]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
18
The Monthly Stop Loss Limit Under CAR-SA
• The monthly stop loss is triggered on a monthly basis 
and is tied to the auction’s maximum clearing price
• The ISO is not proposing any change to the monthly stop 
loss as part of CAR-SA

[Page 19]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
19
The Seasonal Stop-Loss Limit Under CAR-SA
• The move from annual to seasonal auctions requires 
changes to the stop-loss mechanism that corresponds 
with the procurement period
• With the reduction of the procurement period from 12 to 
6 months, the ISO proposes a seasonal stop-loss limit 
that takes the same form as the current annual limit, but 
caps a resource’s seasonal losses at two times its 
maximum monthly net loss

[Page 20]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
20
Key Observations Regarding the Proposed 
Seasonal Stop-Loss Limit
• Results in a lower maximum exposure than if the 
seasonal stop loss continued to be calculated as three 
times a resource’s maximum monthly net loss
• However, we expect it will continue to provide strong 
performance incentives
– To date, no resource would have hit the seasonal stop loss if such a 
design was in place
– For each season, the RAA model suggests that resource adequacy risk 
is primarily concentrated in two months, which aligns with the 
proposed approach

[Page 21]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
21
Conclusion and Next Steps
• Today’s discussion introduced potential approaches to 
address BR capping under CAR-SA
– Stakeholder feedback welcome 
– Proposed approach expected in July
– Please send feedback to Jasleen Singh (jsingh@iso-ne.com) by 
June 24, 2026
• Changes are also proposed to conform the PFP annual 
stop-loss mechanism to a seasonal capacity market

CAR-SA: Capacity Bilaterals and Capacity Exports
WMPP ID:
185
Proposed Effective Date: Q2 2027
• Moving to a prompt market shortens the time horizon over which future 
clearing prices are known
• Participants have expressed interest in an ISO-administered instrument that 
supports capacity price hedging
• Today’s presentation will discuss:
o Relevant background
o Use of a bilateral in price hedging
o Consideration of CLO Bilaterals
o Capacity Internal Bilateral Transaction (Capacity IBT) Proposal
o Capacity Exports

[Page 3]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
RELEVANT BACKGROUND
3

[Page 4]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
4
Relevant Background
• In the Forward Capacity Market (FCM), clearing prices for a 12-month 
commitment period were established when the Forward Capacity Auction (FCA) 
completed, which occurred ~ 40 months prior to the start of the commitment 
period, resulting in clearing prices ~ 40-52 months into the future
• In the prompt, seasonal market, clearing prices for a 6-month season will be 
established ~ 1 month prior to the start of a season, resulting in clearing prices 
~ 1-7 months into the future
• Participants have expressed interest in an ISO-administered instrument that 
supports capacity price hedging (i.e., establishing fixed capacity payments), 
much like Energy Internal Bilateral Transactions do for energy prices
• The ISO assessed this given CAR-SA implementation time constraints

[Page 5]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
USE OF A BILATERAL IN PRICE HEDGING
5

[Page 6]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
6
Use of a Bilateral in Price Hedging
• Participants can hedge price risk using a fixed-for-floating structure in 
which counterparties exchange additional cash flows
• Recall:
– Capacity Load Obligation (CLO): Load’s MW obligation, charged at CLO charge rates
– Capacity Supply Obligation (CSO): Supply’s MW obligation, paid at the clearing 
price
• Because:
– Load Serving Entity (LSE) pays the CLO charge rates, and
– Supply is paid the clearing price,
One party bears the risk of the difference between the CLO charge rates and the clearing price (“basis”)
– If the bilateral references CLO charge rates → supplier bears basis risk
– If it references clearing price → LSE bears basis risk

[Page 7]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
7
Use of a Bilateral in Price Hedging Cont.
•
In addition to the ordinary CLO charges to load and CSO payments to supply, a 
capacity bilateral could be used to achieve the following:
– LSE pays a fixed rate to supply (this would be outside of the ISO, and therefore the ISO would not 
see it or settle it)
– Supply pays a floating rate to LSE (the ISO would settle this)
– Cash flows, including the fixed rate payment that the ISO does not see:
• if floating-rate leg rate = clearing price:
– LSE: floating (floating-rate leg of bilateral) – floating (CLO) – fixed (fixed-rate leg of bilateral) = – fixed – basis
– Supplier: floating (CSO) – floating (floating-rate leg of bilateral) + fixed (fixed-rate leg of bilateral) = fixed
• if floating-rate leg rate = CLO charge rates:
– LSE: floating (floating-rate leg of bilateral) – floating (CLO) – fixed (fixed-rate leg of bilateral) = – fixed
– Supplier: floating (CSO) – floating (floating-rate leg of bilateral) + fixed (fixed-rate leg of bilateral) = fixed – basis

[Page 8]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
CONSIDERATION OF CLO BILATERALS
8

[Page 9]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
9
CLO Bilateral Design
•
A CLO Bilateral is an ISO-administered mechanism that transfers a MW quantity of CLO 
from one Market Participant to another
•
Therefore, a CLO Bilateral can be used to hedge capacity price risk as the floating-rate 
leg of a fixed-for-floating swap structure
•
The transferring participant must have a CLO to transfer
•
A participant without load can acquire CLO via CLO Bilateral
– Allows a supplier to assume capacity charge obligations typically born by an LSE
•
Mechanics:
– LSE pays fixed rate to supplier (the ISO does not see this)
– LSE transfers CLO to supplier via CLO Bilateral
– Supplier pays CLO charge rates on the CLO MW
– Supplier receives payment on its CSO
– Cash flows:
• LSE: – fixed (fixed-rate leg of bilateral) = – fixed
• Supplier: floating (CSO) – floating (CLO Bilateral) + fixed (fixed-rate leg of bilateral) = fixed – basis

[Page 10]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
10
CLO Bilateral Limitations
• The floating rate is limited to CLO charge rates (cannot use clearing 
price)
– Market feedback indicates a preference to use clearing price
• Pricing location is limited to the Capacity Zone of the CLO
• As a result of stakeholder feedback indicating interest in using the 
clearing price and flexibility for selecting pricing Capacity Zone, the ISO 
proposes creating Capacity Internal Bilateral Transactions (IBT), which 
do not have these limitations

[Page 11]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
CAPACITY INTERNAL BILATERAL TRANSACTION 
PROPOSAL
11

[Page 12]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
12
Internal Bilateral Transaction Refresher
• An Internal Bilateral Transaction (IBT) is a mechanism allowing participants to 
transfer financial obligations associated with electricity or capacity between 
one another
• IBT types include:
– Energy
– CLO
• One party transfers, and the other party receives the financial obligation
• The ISO serves as the IBT’s facilitator by transferring the financial obligation 
between parties, but it is not a party to the bilateral contract
• Counterparties attest that the IBT is backed by a physical transfer of electricity 
or MW obligation between them

[Page 13]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
13
Capacity IBT Proposal
• New “Capacity IBT” product implemented within the existing IBT framework
• Could be used as the floating-rate leg of a fixed-for-floating structure (fixed-rate 
leg would not be seen by the ISO)
• Does not transfer CLO or CSO; i.e., it is different from a CLO Bilateral and a CSO 
Bilateral
• One counterparty pays the floating rate and the other receives it
• The ISO serves as the IBT’s facilitator, but it is not a party to the bilateral contract

[Page 14]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
14
Capacity IBT Proposal Cont.
•
Structure:
– Floating rate payer and floating rate receiver
– MW amount by month (may be constant or vary by month)
– Floating rate type (full seasonal clearing price, non-firm gas seasonal clearing price, or CLO charge rates)
– Floating rate location (Capacity Zone)
•
Floating rate is determined by selections made for floating rate type and location
•
Term:
– Start/end dates must start/end on a monthly boundary
– Minimum term: 1 month
– Maximum term: 24 months
•
Submission:
– Earliest: 1 year before the first day of the IBT’s initial month
– Latest: Noon on the first Business Day of the IBT’s initial month
– May be mapped to subaccounts

[Page 15]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
15
Capacity IBT Proposal Cont.
• Financial Assurance (FA):
– Subject to the daily FA credit test for the respective settlement window
– Collateralization requirement ensures the settlement impact of the IBT is covered
– Included in Daily FCM Requirements
• Settlement:
– Follows the capacity market timelines:
• Daily settlement
• Twice-weekly billing and cash flows
– Assuming invoice released before 11 AM:
• Payments from participants due 2 Business Days after invoice
• Remittances to participants made 4 Business Days after invoice
– If a counterparty defaults, then the ISO ceases settling the IBT prospectively
• If the counterparty cures and if the IBT is resubmitted, then the ISO will resume FA requirements 
and settlements

[Page 16]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
16
Capacity IBT Benefits
• Netting within ISO settlements:
– LSE: CLO charge rates are offset by Capacity IBT’s floating-rate credit (not possible if settled 
directly between counterparties)
– Supplier: Capacity IBT’s floating rate charge offset by other ISO credits (not possible if 
settled directly between counterparties)
• Daily settlement with twice-weekly billing and cash flows

[Page 17]
ISO-NE PUBLIC
17
Capacity IBT Example # 1
•
An LSE and a supplier agree to the purchase/sale of capacity at $4/kW-month for 100 MW (fixed)
•
LSE’s CLO = Supplier’s CSO = 100 MW
•
LSE and supplier enter a bilateral that requires the supplier to pay the clearing price (floating); LSE 
assumes the basis risk
•
Seasonal clearing price = $5/kW-month
•
Sum of CLO charge rates = $5.500/kW-month
•
LSE’s monthly cash flows:
CLO = ($5.500) x 1,000 x 100 MW = ($550,000)
Fixed-rate leg of bilateral = ($4) x 1,000 x 100 MW = ($400,000)
Floating-rate leg of bilateral = $5 x 1,000 x 100 MW = $500,000
Net = ($450,000), reflecting fixed rate – basis (i.e., amount by which sum of CLO charge rates exceeds clearing price)
•
Supplier’s monthly cash flows:
CSO = $5 x 1,000 x 100 MW = $500,000
Fixed-rate leg of bilateral = $4 x 1,000 x 100 MW = $400,000
Floating-rate leg of bilateral = ($5) x 1,000 x 100 MW = ($500,000)
Net = $400,000, reflecting fixed rate

• The ISO heard stakeholder feedback on the need for additional price-hedging 
opportunities 
• We have reviewed the potential for CLO Bilaterals to provide price-hedging

• To build on this and provide additional functionality, the ISO proposes to pursue

22

[Page 23]

ISO Proposes to Simplify Rules for Exporting Capacity
• Under the FCM, certain wheeled Export Bids (often referred to as CETICZ) are not 
curtailed during a CSC, which helps participants to export capacity
– Sections III.1.10.7(f) and III.15.8.1.2 are designed for narrow conditions and are therefore rarely 
used, but require significant implementation effort to maintain
• For CAR-SA, the ISO can provide the same functionality with a simpler design 
– Non-CSO exports, Section III.1.10.7(i), are flagged in NEXTT and treated as Regional Network 
Load. They are not curtailed during CSCs if a self-scheduled generator supports them
• OP9 – Scheduling and Dispatch of External Transactions, Section III.C and Appendix B, Section C.2
– Under CAR, instead of Export Bids, participants can submit the opportunity costs of exporting 
capacity for all or a portion of their resource
– Any uncleared Marginal Reliability Impact Capacity (MRIC) will be considered non-CSO and will 
be eligible for the export curtailment priority afforded by III.1.10.7(i)

Draft Tariff Redlines for Proposed Adjustment to the Strike Price

III.1.8.2 Day-Ahead Ancillary Services Strike Price.

(a) For each hour of the Operating Day, the ISO shall specify the Day-Ahead Ancillary Services Strike Price in $/MWh. The value of the Day-Ahead Ancillary Services Strike Price represents an amount that is the greater of the values calculated in accordance with subsections (1) and (2) below:

(1) the greater of (i) $10/MWh greater than a forecast of the expected hourly Real-Time Hub Price for such hour of the Operating Day and (ii) zero; and

(2) a floor value derived in accordance with subsection (c) below.

(b) The forecast used to determine the Day Ahead Ancillary Services Strike Price value calculated in subsection (a)(1) above shall be based on a publicly-available forecasting algorithm developed by the ISO. The ISO shall describe the publicly available forecasting algorithm to Market Participants and shall periodically review and assess the efficacy of the forecasting algorithm. The ISO shall notify stakeholders of any potential revisions to the ISO’s forecasting algorithm prior to implementing such revisions.

(c) In the event that the ISO is not able to utilize the ISO-developed forecasting algorithm described in subsection (b) above due to hardware, software, or telecommunications problems, human error, or exigent circumstances not contemplated by this market rule, the ISO shall determine the Day-Ahead Ancillary Services Strike Price using the best forecast available and shall disclose the use of such substitute forecast to Market Participants as soon as practicable.

(c) The floor value in subsection (a)(2) above shall be determined daily based on the marginal cost of supplying energy by an efficient, distillate-fired combustion turbine generator, reflecting regional emissions costs and the lowest-priced distillate fuel available. The ISO shall describe to Market Participants the heat rate, emissions cost, and fuel prices that it uses to determine the value in subsection (a)(2).

(d) In the event that the ISO is not able to utilize the methods in subsections (a) through (c) above due to hardware, software, or telecommunications problems, human error, or exigent circumstances not contemplated by this market rule, the ISO shall determine the Day-Ahead Ancillary Services Strike Price using the best forecast and floor value available and shall disclose the use of such substitute method to Market Participants as soon as practicable.

III.A.8.1.2. Impact Test.

the threshold prices for failing the conduct test described in Section III.A.8.1.1 for all Day-Ahead Ancillary Services Offers in the hour of the Operating Day being evaluated; and

the Day-Ahead Ancillary Services Benchmark Levels as described in Section III.A.8.2 for all Day-Ahead Ancillary Services Offers in the hour of the Operating Day being evaluated.

III.A.24. 	Deactivation Notification Package Submission and Review.

III.A.24.1.	Deactivation Notifications Requiring Workbook Submission and Review.

A Lead Market Participant seeking to permanently remove all or part of a resource from the Capacity Market or from all New England Markets must follow the Deactivation Notification process pursuant to Section II.52, including the timely and complete submission of a Deactivation Notification Package. For each Deactivation Notification representing the deactivation of greater than 20 MW, the Deactivation Notification Package shall include the cost workbooks and supporting materials described in Section III.A.24.2 for review by the Internal Market Monitor. If more than one Deactivation Notification is submitted by a single Lead Market Participant or its Affiliates (as used in Section III.A.24.6) and the sum of all such Deactivation Notifications in aggregate is greater than 20 MW, then the Lead Market Participant must timely submit each such Deactivation Notification Package, including the cost workbooks and supporting materials described in Section III.A.24.2, as if each deactivation were greater than 20 MW. The Internal Market Monitor has no obligation to review a Deactivation Notification Package if the Deactivation Notification provides notice of either: (a) deactivation of the only resource controlled by a Lead Market Participant or its Affiliates participating in the Capacity Market; or (b) deactivation of all resources controlled by a Lead Market Participant or its Affiliates participating in the Capacity Market, where the term “control” has the meaning set forth in Section III.A.24.6.

Resources requiring review under Section III.A.24.1 that deactivate without submitting the complete information required by Section III.A.24.2 by the Deactivation Notification Deadline set forth in Section II.52.1 may be subject to referral to the Commission’s Office of Enforcement in accordance with Section III.A.19 if the Internal Market Monitor has reason to believe a Market Violation has occurred. In instances where a resource deactivates without submitting the complete information required by Section III.A.24.2, the Internal Market Monitor will determine the Proxy Capacity Offer of the resource pursuant to Section III.A.24.7 and include the Proxy Capacity Offer in the deactivation determinations filing pursuant to Section III.A.24.9.

III.A.24.2.	Submission of Cost Workbooks and Supporting Materials.

Lead Market Participants submitting a Deactivation Notification Package subject to review under Section III.A.24.1 shall submit completed cost workbooks based on the latest Deactivation Notification cost workbooks posted to the ISO’s website. The submitted cost workbooks shall include or be accompanied by sufficient documentation and information about each cost workbook component to allow the Internal Market Monitor to make the requisite determinations regarding their validity and the economic viability of the deactivating resource. Lead Market Participants submitting a Deactivation Notification Package shall include in their submission identifying information relating to all  that the Lead Market Participant and its Affiliates control (as that term is defined in Section III.A.24.6) including all capacity the control of which it has contracted to a third party.

Lead Market Participants may elect to submit the relevant cost workbooks and supporting materials for a completeness determination by the Internal Market Monitor  no later than 30 days before the Deactivation Notification Deadline. No later than ten business days before the Deactivation Notification Deadline, the Internal Market Monitor shall notify those Lead Market Participants submitting materials for a completeness determination that either: (a) the submission has been determined to be complete; or (b) the submission has been determined to be incomplete, and identifying any aspects of the workbook or supporting materials that are deemed incomplete. Submission of a cost workbook and supporting materials for a completeness determination is optional and does not eliminate the requirement to submit a Deactivation Notification and Deactivation Notification Package on or immediately before the Deactivation Notification Deadline.

III.A.24.3.	Internal Market Monitor Review of Deactivation Notification Package.

The Internal Market Monitor shall review all Deactivation Notification Packages requiring review pursuant to Section III.A.24.1 that the Internal Market Monitor determines contain a complete submission of cost workbooks and supporting material submitted on or before the Deactivation Notification Deadline for the relevant Capacity Commitment Period. The Internal Market Monitor is under no obligation to review Deactivation Notifications that it deems to be incomplete at the time of the Deactivation Notification Deadline due to incomplete cost workbooks and supporting materials.

The Internal Market Monitor shall review each timely-submitted and complete Deactivation Notification Package requiring review pursuant to Section III.A.24.1 to determine whether the economic basis for the deactivation is consistent with: (1) the net present value of the resource’s expected cash flows (as determined pursuant to Section III.A.24.4.1); (2) reasonable expectations about the resource’s Capacity Performance Payments (as determined pursuant to Section III.A.24.4.2); and (3) the resource’s reasonable opportunity costs (as determined pursuant to Section III.A.24.4.3).  The Internal Market Monitor shall review all relevant information (including data, studies, and assumptions) to determine whether the submission is consistent with the resource’s net going forward costs, reasonable expectations about the resource’s Capacity Performance Payments, and reasonable opportunity costs. In making this determination, the Internal Market Monitor shall consider, among other things, industry standards, market conditions (including published indices and projections), resource-specific characteristics and conditions, portfolio size, and consistency of assumptions across that portfolio.

The Internal Market Monitor may seek additional information from the Lead Market Participant (including information about the other existing or potential new resources controlled by the Lead Market Participant) after the Deactivation Notification Deadline for resources requiring review under Section III.A.24 to address any questions or concerns regarding the data submitted, as appropriate.

III.A.24.4.	Net Present Value of Expected Cash Flows.

For those Capacity Resources subject to Internal Market Monitor review pursuant to Section III.A.24.1, the net present value of a Capacity Resource’s expected cash flows shall be determined as described in this Section III.A.24.4.

III.A.24.4.1.	Net Present Value of Expected Cash Flows Formula.

The Lead Market Participant for a Capacity Resource that submits a Deactivation Notification that is to be reviewed by the Internal Market Monitor shall report all expected costs, revenues, prices, discount rates and capital expenditures in a manner and format specified by the Internal Market Monitor, and may supplement this information with other evidence. The Internal Market Monitor will review the Lead Market Participant’s submitted data to ensure that it is consistent with overall market conditions and reflects expected values. The Internal Market Monitor will adjust any data that are inconsistent with overall market conditions or do not reflect expected values. The Internal Market Monitor shall enter all relevant expected costs, revenues, prices, discount rates and capital expenditures into a capital budgeting model and shall determine the net present value of the Capacity Resource’s expected cash flows as follows:

The net present value of the Capacity Resource’s expected cash flows is equal to (i) the net present value of the Capacity Resource’s net expected cash flows over the resource’s remaining economic life (as determined below) plus the net present value of the resource’s expected terminal value, using the resource’s discount rate, divided by (ii) the product of the resource’s Capacity (in kilowatts) and months.

The Capacity Resource’s net expected cash flow for Capacity Commitment Period of the resource’s remaining economic life (i.e., the Capacity Commitment Period associated with the Deactivation Notification) is the resource’s expected net operating profit, including expected capacity revenues, less its expected capital expenditures in the Capacity Commitment Period.

Where:

Expected net operating profit, in dollars, is the Lead Market Participant’s expected profit that might otherwise be avoided or not accrued if the resource were not subject to the obligations of a  apacity esource during the Capacity Commitment Period. Expected labor, maintenance, taxes, insurance, administrative and other normal expenses that can be avoided or not incurred if the resource is deactivated may be included. Service of debt is not an avoidable cost and may not be included.

Expected capacity revenues, in dollars, are the forecasted expected capacity revenues based on the Lead Market Participant’s forecasted expected capacity prices for each of the subsequent Capacity Commitment Periods of the resource’s remaining economic life. The Lead Market Participant shall provide the Internal Market Monitor with documentation supporting the forecasted expected capacity prices. The supporting documentation must include a detailed description and sources of the Lead Market Participant’s assumptions about expected resource additions, resource deactivations, estimated Installed Capacity Requirements, estimated Local Sourcing Requirements, expected market conditions, and any other assumptions used to develop the forecasted expected capacity prices in each Capacity Commitment Period.

If the Internal Market Monitor determines the Lead Market Participant has not provided adequate supporting documentation for the forecasted expected capacity prices, the Internal Market Monitor will replace the Lead Market Participant’s forecasted expected capacity prices with the Internal Market Monitor’s estimate thereof in each Capacity Commitment Period of the resource’s remaining economic life.

Expected capital expenditures, in dollars, are the Lead Market Participant’s expected capital investments that might otherwise be avoided or not incurred if the resource were not subject to the obligations of a listed capacity resource during the Capacity Commitment Periods.

Expected terminal value, in dollars, for resources with five years or less of remaining economic life, is the Lead Market Participant’s expected revenue less expected costs associated with deactivating the resource. For resources with more than five years of remaining economic life, the expected terminal value in the fifth year of the evaluation period is the Lead Market Participant’s expected revenue less expected costs associated with deactivating the resource at the end of the resource’s economic life plus the net present value of the Capacity Resource’s net expected cash flows from the sixth year of the evaluation period through the end of the resource’s remaining economic life, using the resource’s discount rate.

Discount rate is a value reflecting the Lead Market Participant’s weighted average cost of capital for the Capacity Resource adjusted to reflect the risk to cash flows calculated pursuant to the net present value of expected cash flows analysis in this Section III.A.24.4.

The Lead Market Participant shall provide the Internal Market Monitor with documentation supporting the weighted average cost of capital for the Capacity Resource adjusted for risk. The supporting documentation must include a detailed description and sources of the Lead Market Participant’s assumptions associated with the cost of capital, risks and any other assumptions used to develop the weighted average cost of capital for the Capacity Resource adjusted for risk. If the Internal Market Monitor determines the Lead Market Participant has not provided adequate supporting documentation for the weighted average cost of capital for the Capacity Resource adjusted for risk, the Lead Market Participant has included risks not associated with cash flows calculated pursuant to the net present value of expected cash flows analysis in this Section III.A.24.4 or the Lead Market Participant has submitted costs, revenues, capital expenditures or prices that are not reflective of expected values, the Internal Market Monitor will replace the Lead Market Participant’s discount rate with a value determined by the Internal Market Monitor.

The Internal Market Monitor shall calculate the Capacity Resource’s remaining economic life, using evaluation periods ranging from one to  the Capacity Commitment Period the Deactivation Notification. For each evaluation period, the Internal Market Monitor will calculate the net present value of (a) the expected net operating profit minus expected capital expenditures assuming the Capacity Clearing Price for the first is equal to the Internal Market Monitor’s estimate of the Capacity Auction Offer Price Cap and (b) the expected terminal value of the resource at the end of the given evaluation period. The economic life is the evaluation period in which a resource’s net present value is maximized.

III.A.24.4.2.	Expected Capacity Performance Payments.

The Lead Market Participant for a Capacity Resource that submits a Deactivation Notification that is to be reviewed by the Internal Market Monitor shall also provide documentation separately detailing the expected Capacity Performance Payments for the resource. This documentation must include expectations regarding the applicable Capacity Balancing Ratio, the number of hours of reserve deficiency, and the resource’s performance during reserve deficiencies.

III.A.24.4.3.	Opportunity Costs.

To the extent that a Capacity Resource submitting Deactivation Notification has additional opportunity costs that are not reflected in the net going forward costs, net present value of expected cash flows, expected Capacity Performance Payments, discount rate, or risk premium components of the bid, the Lead Market Participant must include evidence supporting such costs. Opportunity costs associated with major repairs necessary to restore decreases in capacity, capital projects required to operate the plant as a capacity resource or for other uses of the resource shall be considered, provided such costs are substantiated by evidence of a repair plan, documented business plan and fundamental market analysis, or other independent and transparent trading index or indices as applicable. Substantiation of opportunity costs relying on sales in reconfiguration auctions or risk aversion premiums shall not be considered sufficient justification.

III.A.24.4.4.	Stations Having Common Costs.

Deactivation Notifications submitted by a Generating Capacity Resource that is associated with a Station having Common Costs and seeking to deactivate must include detailed cost data to allow the ISO to determine the Asset-Specific Going Forward Costs for each asset associated with the Station and the Station Going Forward Common Costs. The Internal Market Monitor will review each Deactivation Notification from a Generating Capacity Resource that is associated with a Station having Common Costs pursuant to the following methodology:

Calculate the average Asset-Specific Going Forward Costs of each asset at the Station.

Order the assets from highest average Asset-Specific Going Forward Costs to lowest average Asset-Specific Going Forward Costs; this is the preferred deactivation order.

Calculate and assign to each asset a station cost that is equal to the average cost of the assets remaining at the Station, including Station Going Forward Common Costs, assuming the successive deactivation of each individual asset in preferred deactivation order.

Calculate a set of composite costs that is equal to the maximum of the cost associated with each asset as calculated in (i) and (iii) above.

The Internal Market Monitor will adjust the set of composite costs to ensure a monotonically nonincreasing set of prices as follows: any asset with a composite cost that is greater than the composite cost of the asset with the lowest composite cost and that has average Asset-Specific Going Forward Costs that are less than its composite costs will have its composite cost set equal to that of the asset with the lowest composite cost. The price of the asset with the lowest composite cost and of any assets whose composite costs are so adjusted will be considered a single non-rationable bid for use in the Capacity Auction.

The Internal Market Monitor will compare a price developed using the adjusted composite costs to the Deactivation Notification submitted by the Generating Capacity Resource that is associated with a Station having Common Costs. If the Internal Market Monitor determines that the submitted price is greater than the price developed using the adjusted composite costs or is not consistent with the submitted supporting cost data, then the Internal Market Monitor will establish an Internal Market Monitor-calculated price as described in Section  III.A.24.5 and, if the resource is determined to be deactivating to the benefit of a portfolio pursuant to III.A.24.6, the Internal Market Monitor shall use the Internal Market Monitor calculated price as the Proxy Capacity Offer Price pursuant to III.A.24.7.

III.A.24.5.	Conduct Test.

The Internal Market Monitor shall review those Deactivation Notifications submitted pursuant to Section III.A.24.1 to determine whether the economic basis for a Deactivation Notification and associated cost workbooks are consistent with the reasonable net present value of the resource’s expected cash flows, reasonable expectations about the resource’s Capacity Performance Payments, and the resource’s reasonable opportunity costs.

After due consideration and consultation with the Lead Market Participant, as appropriate, the Internal Market Monitor shall calculate a break-even price based on the Internal Market Monitor’s reasonable expectations regarding net present value of the resource’s expected cash flows, the resource’s Capacity Performance Payments, and the resource’s opportunity costs. If the expected Capacity Clearing Price is more than 10% greater than the break-even price, then that resource fails the conduct test.

For those resources failing the conduct test, the Internal Market Monitor shall perform a further review of the Lead Market Participant’s portfolio pursuant to III.A.24.6.

III.A.24.6.	Portfolio Benefit Test.

The portfolio benefit test is performed for each Lead Market Participant submitting a Deactivation Notification subject to review  Section III.A.24.5. The test will be performed as follows:

If

The capacity revenue from the Lead Market Participant’s total , not including the associated with the Deactivation Notification, is greater than

the capacity revenue from the Lead Market Participant’s total , including the associated with the Deactivation Notifications for resources controlled by the Lead Market Participant that the conduct test as calculated pursuant to subsection v. below, then

the Lead Market Participant will be found to have a portfolio benefit pursuant to the portfolio benefit test.

Where,

the Lead Market Participant’s capacity revenue from the Lead Market Participant’s total not including the associated with the Deactivation Notification is calculated as the product of (a) the Lead Market Participant’s total  not including theassociated with the Deactivation Notification that the subject of the review and (b) the Internal Market Monitor-simulated Capacity Clearing Price not including the associated with the Deactivation Notification

The Lead Market Participant’s capacity revenue from the Lead Market Participant’s total including the associated with the Deactivation Notification is calculated as the product of (a) the Lead Market Participant’s total  including the associated with the Deactivation Notification  and (b) the Internal Market Monitor-simulated Capacity Clearing Price including the associated with the Deactivation Notification.

For purposes of subsections iv. and v. above, the Internal Market Monitor-simulated Capacity Clearing Price, not to exceed the Capacity Auction Offer Price Cap, is based on  the System-Wide Capacity Demand Curve, Capacity Zone Demand Curves, and the supply  developed from the most recent Capacity Auction.

For purposes of the test performed in this Section III.A.24, the of a Lead Market Participant includes the capacity of Capacity Resources that are controlled by the Lead Market Participant or its Affiliates.

For purposes of determining the  of a Lead Market Participant or its Affiliates under this Section III.A.24, “control” or “controlled” means the possession, directly or indirectly, of the authority to direct the decision-making regarding how capacity is offered into the Capacity Market, and includes control by contract with unaffiliated third parties. In complying with Section I.3.5 of the ISO Tariff, a Lead Market Participant shall inform the ISO of all capacity that it and its Affiliates control under this Section III.A.24.6 and all capacity the control of which it has contracted to a third party.

III.A.24.7.	Proxy Capacity Offer.

For those deactivations the Internal Market Monitor determines havethe portfolio benefit test set forth in Section III.A.24.6, The deactivation determination filing made to the Commission as described in Section III.A.24.9 shall include an explanation of the resource’s Proxy Capacity Offer price. Unless the Commission determines otherwise, the ISO shall enter Proxy Capacity Offers into the Capacity Auction pursuant to Section III.15.4.

III.A.24.8.	Deactivation Determination Notification.

No later than 90 days after Deactivation Notification Deadline, the Internal Market Monitor shall provide written notification to the Lead Market Participant that submitted each Deactivation Notification concerning the result of the Internal Market Monitor’s conduct test conducted pursuant to Section III.A.24.5.

III.A.24.9.	Deactivation Determinations Filing.

No later than 120 days after Deactivation Notification Deadline, the ISO shall make a filing with the Commission pursuant to Section 205 of the Federal Power Act confidentially describing the determinations made by the Internal Market Monitor with respect to each Deactivation Notification failing the conduct test, including the supporting documentation for each such determination. The filing shall identify to the extent possible the components of the Deactivation Notification which were accepted as justified, and shall also identify to the extent possible the components of the Deactivation Notification which were not justified and which resulted in the Internal Market Monitor identifying the resource as requiring a Proxy Capacity Offer. The deactivation determinations filing shall identify the Proxy Capacity Offer price that, pursuant to Section III.15.4, will be entered into the Capacity Auction during the Capacity Commitment Period in question if the Commission accepts the deactivation determinations filing.  In the event that no Deactivation Notification failed the conduct test associated with a particular Deactivation Notification Deadline, the filing shall state that outcome.

In the event that a Lead Market Participant elects pursuant to Section II.53 to delay a resource’s deactivation for reliability reasons, and elects pursuant to Section II.54.1 to be compensated based on net going forward costs, the deactivation determinations filing shall include a description of the resource’s net going forward costs and all supporting materials necessary to arrive at the resource’s net going forward costs, including a description of any instances in which the Internal Market Monitor-determined net going forward costs differ from the net going forward costs that may be arrived at based solely on the resource’s cost workbook submission.

Capacity Offer Price Threshold (COPT) 
Methodology
• The COPT methodology is conformed from the Dynamic 
Delist Bid Threshold (DDBT) methodology from the FCA
• The calculation of the COPT is to average the capacity 
price from the previous main auction with the price on the 
upcoming auction’s system demand curve at the same 
quantity of CSO that cleared in the prior primary auction,
– subject to upper and lower limits (no lower than 25% of Net CONE 
or higher than 75% of Net CONE for the upcoming auction) and the 
addition of an “adder”
– The Appendix includes a slide on the equations
• The ISO is planning on using this COPT methodology in 
CAR-SA

Current Thinking of the Initial-COPT 
Methodology for CCP19
• However, given the ISO has never conducted a prompt 
MRIC based auction before, there is no “first capacity 
price” from an auction to use in the COPT calculation for 
CCP19 
• Instead, for the first summer/winter capacity auctions in 
CCP19, the ISO is proposing to implement an initial COPT 
• Current thinking is that the initial COPT will be one number 
for both the summer and winter seasons 
• To derive the number, the current thinking is to multiply the 
CCP19 annual Net CONE adjusted for MRIC by 37%
• 37% is derived from the average of dividing the DDBT prices with the 
annual Net CONE prices from FCA16-18 
– The Appendix includes the calculation

methodology will be applied within each season
– e.g, the winter season COPT is the average of the previous winter 
season’s capacity price with the expected winter capacity price 
corresponding to the cleared CSO quantity from the previous 
winter season 
• With the transition mechanism the ISO is proposing for 
implementing CAR-SA, the ISO may need to adjust the 
COPT to reflect the transition mechanism
• Details on what that would look like for the COPT is still 
being considered

Definition of the Pivotal Supplier Test
•
A market participant (Ultimate Parent Company) is pivotal if 
some quantity of the participant’s portfolio is needed to meet a 
locational capacity requirement
– Net ICR (for system level requirement), Local Sourcing Requirement 
(for an import constrained Capacity Zone)
•
For example, (assuming away Capacity Zones for simplicity), 
suppose Net ICR is 9000 MWs, "UPC A’s" portfolio is 1000 MWs
– If all other non-UPC A participants control 8500 MWs, then UPC A is a 
pivotal supplier
Without UPC A's capacity, the system cannot satisfy the Net ICR
– If all other non-UPC A participants control 9100 MWs, then UPC A is 
not a pivotal supplier
•
For capacity located behind an export constraint, capacity is 
treated as non-pivotal if there are sufficient resources behind 
the constraint offered by other participants such that, even after 
removing the UPC's MWs from the export constrained zone, the 
interface limit is binding

How the Pivotal Supplier Test is Applied in 
the Auction
•
The ISO is not planning on making any material changes to the 
pivotal supplier test 
•
The pivotal supplier test is conducted once all Capacity Offers 
have been submitted
– Any Capacity Offer segments that exceed the Allowable Capacity Offer 
Price, and is considered pivotal, will be automatically lowered to the 
Allowable Capacity Offer Price associated with that segment  in the 
auction
•
If a resource is mitigated, the Lead Market Participant will be 
informed promptly upon completion of the auction
•
As introduced in CAR-PD, if a participant believes a resource 
will not be able to recover the costs of providing CSO as a result 
of being improperly mitigated, the participant may seek cost 
recovery from FERC

Supplier Test Design
• Introduction of gas constraint effectively creates a new 
type of export constrained "zone"
– Like other export constrained zones, capacity located behind the 
gas constraint is less able to raise clearing prices through 
economic withholding than capacity in front of the constraint 
• For the purposes of the pivotal supplier test, the ISO is 
planning to treat the non-firm gas constraint analogously 
to an export constrained Capacity Zone

Discussion
•
What happens if a resource does not take on a CSO and their 
NBA is to temporarily exit the energy markets?
– If the resource does not take on a CSO and their NBA is to temporarily 
exit, the resource would presumably not operate for the season 
• Though the resource could always enter the monthly reconfiguration 
auction if expectations of costs or revenues changed
•
Would not clearing one season impact the resource’s offer in 
the following season
– Offer formulation is generally independent from CCP to CCP. Offers, 
like operational decisions, are expected to be forward-looking
• Offers are based on avoidable costs, net E&AS revenues, and expectations 
of PFP for that specific CCP 
• Capital costs that are incorporated into offers must be avoidable for the 
upcoming CCP
• In the seasonal construct, there could be a case where a resource might 
incorporate a portion of their annual costs into the seasonal offer, for 
which the cost is avoidable

• Would not clearing one season impact the resource’s offer 
in the following season
– If a resource fully operates in the energy markets with or without a

their offer for the next season
• The resource would still incur the same costs for the first season 
regardless of their CSO status 
– However, if a resource required a CSO to fully participate in the 
energy markets in the first season, it could impact their second 
season offer to the extent their avoidable GFCs changed
• For example, if the resource avoided undertaking a maintenance 
procedure after the first season because of not clearing

Gas Resources who Partially Firm
•
Gas resources might elect to offer some but not all their MWs as 
firm (i.e., partially firm)
– See the April 2026 MC
•
When a resource offers both non-firm and firm MWs into the 
auction, they can offer their MWs in three ways:
(i)   the non-firm and firm MWs are offered at the same price
(ii)  the non-firm MWs are offered at a higher price than the firm MWs 
(iii) the non-firm MWs are offered at a lower price than the firm MWs 
•
As discussed, optimal offers should reflect the resource’s NBA. 
For resources that partially firm their MWs, the optimal offer 
price for the firm and non-form segments should likewise reflect 
the resource’s NBA for each of those segments

• The ISO’s proposal is consistent with the initial thinking

• The core review process will remain unchanged from

Treatment of Capacity Once it Receives a 
CSO in a Seasonal Capacity Auction
• Once a quantity of capacity receives a CSO in a seasonal 
capacity auction, that quantity will not be subject to a floor 
price in future like-season auctions
– For example, consider a resource subject to a floor price that is 
qualified for 10 MWs of MRIC in summer, 12 MWs of MRIC in winter
– Suppose the resource sold 6 MWs of MRIC in a summer capacity 
auction
• In future summer capacity auctions, the resource would be able to 
offer up to 6 MWs of capacity not subject to an offer floor
• The remaining 4 MWs of summer MRIC and 12 MWs of winter MRIC 
would remain subject to an offer floor

Full Recalculation of Floor Prices
• This process exists in the current CAR-PD rules, will 
be retained for CAR-SA (as presented to August 2025 MC)
• If a participant believes the underlying economics facing 
the resource have sufficiently changed from those 
described in the BSMP package, it can request a "full 
recalculation" from the IMM
– Effectively, the IMM will start from the ground up and reexamine the 
resource's development costs, relevant costs and revenues, and 
assumptions
– Result is a "new" necessary capacity revenue value for any 
capacity that remains subject to an offer floor

For any resource's MRIC that have received a CSO in a primary 
capacity auction, the IMM will account for these MWs' annualized 
capacity revenue

Application of BSMP to Incremental 
Additions of Capacity
• As in CAR-PD, BSMP reviews may be required for 
incremental additions of capacity at a resource that has 
previously supplied CSO
– Only an incremental addition arising from a material modification 
to the resource will be potentially subject to BSMP
– Excludes an MRIC increase arising from, for example, higher MCap 
from improved operations of a resource or a higher rMRI value
• BSMP reviews for incremental capacity will follow the 
same underlying procedure as described for new 
developments
– Only projects that do not satisfy either lane 1 or lane 2 exclusions 
might face an offer floor

[Page 2]
Summary of Amendments
• Amendment 1—Weather Year Weighting Adjustment: ISO’s weather-year weighting proposal may 
overstate the frequency of sustained winter cold snaps that drive storage derating.
• Conceptual Amendment: ISO should replace peak-day weighting of tail events with multi-day event 
metrics that capture the duration of consecutive days, which better represent winter cold-snaps.
• Amendment 2—Intertie Modeling: ISO’s proposed flat import-capacity block may understate the 
timing of import deliveries that support critical storage charging. 
• Conceptual Amendment: ISO should use neighboring system operators load shapes capturing hourly 
import profiles for the intertie that reflect when energy is actually available and likely to be delivered.

[Page 3]
Why We Are Bringing Amendments
• ISO-NE’s seasonal accreditation reforms will shape whether the capacity market sends an 
appropriate investment signal for flexible resources like storage and DR.
• The capacity market can only send efficient investment signals and spur the build out of flexible 
resources if capacity accreditation fairly values resources. ISO’s proposal may fail to support 
efficient investment, steer new resource entry away from New England, and raise concerns over 
resource adequacy, clean energy targets, and affordability. 
• Accreditation should measure expected reliability contribution under realistic system 
conditions that reflects real-world operations, behaviors, and inputs.

[Page 4]
Amendment 1:
Weather Year Weighting 
Adjustment

[Page 5]
Amendment 1: Weather Year Weighting Adjustment
•
Key point—ISO’s proposal overlooks timing and duration of events, which matters for weighting: For 
weighting weather years, the ISO proposes to use full historical profiles based on their contribution to the 
high daily peak-load distribution, rather than based on the frequency of the multi-day cold-snap blocks
within those years. Peak load days are only a single dimension of many that influence adequacy and 
accreditation, so using that alone leads to a misleading weighting for selecting winter weather in the 
context of how it impacts resource adequacy. The timing and duration of those extreme cold days matter at 
least as much if not more. 
•
ISO’s approach likely over-states winter risk: ISO proposes to weigh the 2003/2004 weather year as a 
2.71% probability, and that year accounts for a significant portion of overall EUE (which drives MRI values). 
Yet, as FirstLight demonstrates, the probability of a multi-day (e.g. 5 days) cold weather event in that year is 
far less than 2.71%, suggesting ISO’s proposal overweighs that year. 
•
Result of ISO’s proposal—storage disproportionately penalized: Energy storage in particular will be 
undervalued if the model improperly assumes more frequent/severe long-duration reliability events than is 
realistic. The more severe or frequent the extended cold-snap, the fewer opportunities storage has to 
charge, making storage less available during MRI hours and lowering its MRIC value.

[Page 6]
Amendment 1: Weather Year Weighting Adjustment
• Conceptual amendment: ISO should adjust its weather year weighting according 
to how frequently multi-day events occur, not based on distributions of peak load 
days (which may be isolated/spread apart). Capturing the temporal/durational 
component of cold days in weather year weighting is a crucial input to a fair and 
accurate weighting since in winter, the primary driver of EUE (and MRIC values) is 
during multi-day cold-snaps. 
• FirstLight’s proposal for the 5 coldest 5-day cold blocks seems reasonable, but 
United is open to any metric that better captures the temporal and durational 
elements of the cold weather events.

[Page 7]
Amendment 2:
Intertie Modeling

[Page 8]
Amendment 2: Intertie Modeling
• ISO’s modeled ties underestimate charging opportunities for storage: The 
proposed flat block of capacity overlooks the empirical profile of those ties, i.e. when 
energy from that tie is actually being delivered, which is often overnight and—
critically—in-between Type 3 MRI hours, which would allow storage to recharge.
• Firm capacity (estimated as the tie benefit) is treated as a thermal unit ‘at the border’ 
– the key point is that the value of the tie is proxied as a flat block of firm capacity 
akin to any other thermal generator (with no fuel limitations).
• Ties may be constrained during coincident peak winter scarcity events, but may have 
more ability and incentive to deliver overnight when ISO-NE prices are very high. This 
could turn one modeled 96-hour duration event into several shorter events, 
materially improving storage rMRI and better reflecting real-world operations.

[Page 9]
Amendment 2: Intertie Modeling
•
Model assumes flat profile: ISO models imports as part of a ‘firm’ block of thermals/imports with an 
effectively flat profile across the day (grey wedge bottom of the graphic). 
•
Flattening that profile into a capacity block may obscure the hours when imports are actually available 
(which will often exceed the flat profile), such as overnight hours that may allow storage to recharge.

would otherwise recharge. Note: hourly HQ export capability shown is representative, not actual, for a critical period.
•
The key is that the ISO proposal converts an import shape that should have more energy available during off peak into 
an equivalent flat block (green line) and this underestimates energy available from the interties.

Amendment 2: Intertie Modeling
Profiled Export Availability vs Flat Block
• Takeaway—ISO proposal fails to capture temporal profile/hourly shape of the intertie: The 
key issue is that the ISO approach creates a system with a flat import profile during critical 
periods, whereas the realistic profile would have increased import availability in off-peak 
hours, thereby allowing more storage to be charged than the flat profile.
• ISO’s proposal underestimates energy available for charging storage off-peak: ISO’s 
proposal converts an import shape that should have more energy available during off peak 
hours (striped blue shading, prior slide) into an equivalent flat block (green line) and this under-
estimates the available energy for charging storage. The figure, a simplification, illustrates HQ 
would have more export capacity potential overnight. 
• Conceptual amendment: Model firm imports using the underlying hourly import-availability 
profile of the tie, aligned with load and scarcity conditions, rather than converting that profile 
into a flat firm capacity block that ignores when imports are actually available to serve load or

estimated from the underlying regional system model results.

Appendix: 
Other Issues

[Page 14]
EUE vs LOLE 
in Assessing MRIC

[Page 15]
EUE vs LOLE in Assessing MRIC
• Issue: Leading accreditation modeling expert espoused in a post that the reliability metric used for resource 
adequacy must be the same that determines accreditation, otherwise it will undercount storage and overlook their 
capacity contribution. ISO-NE uses LOLE for RAA, but then uses EUE for determining MRI, which could be 
undervaluing storage. 
• Request: test if there is a conceptual concern with mixing measures between resource adequacy and resource 
accreditation. In particular, the concern is that by using EUE to assess capacity value and LOLE to set the reliability 
target, ISO is creating an inconsistent and unfair outcome for some asset types.
• Proposed test: for the near term scenario (winter as an example), take the base results and assume 100 MW of load 
growth beyond the ‘at criteria’ load. Based on ISO results for MRIC, this incremental load could logically be met by 
approximately 500 MW of storage (rMRI ~ 0.19, with small adjustment for NICR). If there is no disconnect introduced 
by the ISO approach, we would expect that adding 500 MW of storage to meet 100 MW incremental load would 
maintain approximately the same level of reliability as measured by LOLE. If Kevin Carden is correct, we would expect 
that the reliability value of storage is under-stated because accreditation is tied to EUE, and as a result the LOLE 
would fall below 0.05 when the implied amount of storage is used to meet the load growth. In essence, because the 
storage is under-valued, reliability as measured by LOLE would improve.
• Implication: if the system is exactly at criteria in 2030 for example, and load grows by 100 MW for the 2031 auction, 
MRIC sends a misleading signal because adding 500 MW of storage additions would cause the system to exceed 
criteria. If true, this is a result of the mismatch in the reliability metric and the accreditation signal. It also implies 
storage is being under-paid relative to meeting the reliability criteria.

[Page 16]
Measuring MCAP via 
Average vs. Best 
Performance

[Page 17]
Amendment: Measuring MCAP via Average vs. Best Performance
• Issue: ISO’s proposed MCAP approach appears to rely on a resource’s best observed 
performance during a normalized seasonal temperature window. A single best output 
may reflect an unusually favorable operating hour, not expected performance during 
stressed conditions.
• This could inflate MCAP for some resources and increase MRI values relative to 
resources modeled on more representative expected performance.
• Inconsistent with solar, ADR, profiled resources, and DCAP-limited resources, which
appear linked to expected performance under historical profiles, not one best output.

[Page 18]
Amendment: Measuring MCAP via Average vs. Best Performance
• Data Request: ISO-NE should provide the difference between MCAP and DCAP at a 
system level.  DCAP appears to more fundamentally measure expected availability in 
critical hours as compared to MCAP. 
• Conceptual amendment: Replace MCAP with DCAP so that expected performance 
on peak demand days is based on either actual generation or ECOMAX (adjusted by 
performance factor).
• This would still measure demonstrated performance when the resource was called 
upon, but would avoid anchoring accreditation to one best historical hour.
• ISO will need to solve how to identify when a generator is being fully dispatched so 
that performance datapoint is included in the average MCAP calculation.

[Page 19]
DR Profile Composition 
Flexibility

[Page 20]
Amendment: DR Profile Composition Flexibility
• Issue: Demand Response asset composition can change significantly year to year, 
but ISO’s profile methodology may not reflect those changes quickly enough.
• Core concern: if a DR provider drops poor performers and enrolls stronger 
customers, the DRA’s historical profile may still reflect the old customer mix. This 
could suppress rMRI even when the current portfolio is more reliable or better 
aligned with MRI hours.
• The market should reward DR providers for improving portfolio quality, targeting 
better load flexibility, and enrolling customers that can perform during reliability-risk 
hours.
• Amendment: Afford DR Providers greater flexibility and optionality to update the 
composition of their DERA and and update their rMRI values in timely manner.
